News.title: Leicester church fire LIVE: Huge flames take hold of historic building
News.content:
Firefighters are tackling the blaze at the church in the city centre as local residents have been warned to close all doors and windows as thick smoke fills the sky

A UK city centre church is in flames as huge clouds of smoke fill the sky.

St Andrews Church in Leicester is reportedly alight on Wednesday morning.

The building on Jarrom Street is ablaze with fire crews rushing to the scene to tackle the bright red flames and control the thick smoke.

A spokesperson for Leicestershire Fire and Rescue Control said: "There is an incident on Jarrom Street in Leicester City, this is sending smoke over the city. Please keep windows and doors closed!"

This is a live news story, follow below for further updates.

News.title: Landslide kills at least one person at Solomon Islands gold mine, police say
News.content:
Landslide kills at least one person at Solomon Islands gold mine, police say

On Monday July 27 a landslide struck the open pit mine on Guadalcanal, the largest island of the South Pacific nation - a man's body has now been recovered from the site

View 2 Images The site, near the capital Honiara, is the country's only large-scale gold mine. (Image: Chrisnrita Aumanu Leong/ABC via)

A man’s body has been recovered from the site of a landslide at a gold mine in Solomon Islands, officials said.

‌



On Monday July 27 a landslide struck the open pit mine on Guadalcanal, the largest island of the South Pacific nation. Just 24 hours later the body of a man was recovered from the site.

‌



The slip spanned 100 meters (328 feet) on an access road leading to the pit, the statement said. The cause of the landslide wasn’t known, Prime Minister Matthew Wale told reporters on Monday. It is not known if other people were buried at the site so a search operation is ongoing, police said in a statement.

‌



View 2 Images The man killed was named by police as Ashley Olo, but officials didn't specify if he was a mine worker.

Terrifying wildfire map shows UK towns and cities that would be hit the hardest READ MORE :

Mr Wale said: "Of interest to the government, of course, is to find out whether this was a result of poor mining practices and perhaps the need to strengthen regulations." At the time he said no one was confirmed missing or killed.

‌



The mine’s owners, Wanguo Gold Group Ltd, said in a statement Monday that none of their employees were hurt or missing and no mining equipment was damaged. Operations at the mine had resumed, the statement said.

The man killed was named by police as Ashley Olo, but officials didn't specify if he was a mine worker. Olo's body was returned to his family, said police Acting Commissioner James Aitorea.

According to local news outlets, some families reported people as missing who were not employees of the mine but so-called informal miners operating there. Local reports said the site has attracted controversy before, when local landowners and illegal miners clashed with law enforcement.

Article continues below

The site, near the capital Honiara, is the country's only large-scale gold mine. Operated by Gold Ridge Mining Limited, the mine has since 2019 been majority-owned by the Hong Kong-listed, Chinese-headquartered firm Wanguo Gold Group, with local landowners holding a small stake, Australian Broadcasting Corp. reported.

It was previously owned by an Australian company, which sold the mine in 2015 because of fears it was unsafe in flooding and other natural disasters.

News.title: Japan earthquake live: Death toll climbs to 13 as rescue efforts continue
News.content:
Part of the compound of the Shohinken garden is seen damaged in Yatsushiro, Kumamoto Prefecture, on July 29

Multiple people have died while more are missing after a shopping centre collapsed following a huge 7.1 magnitude earthquake on the Japanese island of Kyushu

A major magnitude-7.1 earthquake struck the Japanese island of Kyushu on Tuesday, according to Japan's meteorological survey.

The quaketoppled buildings, sparked fires, brought down part of an ancient castle and even triggered an explosion at a popular shopping centre.

13 people have been confirmed dead, including two women who were at an Aeon Mall shopping centre in Kumamoto prefecture, where the explosion occurred following the massive earthquake.

Multiple people remain missing at the nearby Nippon Paper Industries Yatsushiro Plant, where the tip of a chimney fell down, national broadcaster NHK has reported.

The massive quake measured at the highest possible level seven on Japan's own Shindo "scale of shaking".

This is an ongoing incident. Check back as the day progresses for further updates.

News.title: M1 traffic LIVE: Busy motorway closed near Luton airport after 'oil spill'
News.content:
Police have closed the motorway near Luton following the incident, which involved multiple vehicles and has created an oil spill which requires specialist clean up

Police have closed part of the M1 near Luton after a huge multi-vehicle crash caused an oil spillage.

The southbound side of the motorway has been closed between junctions 11 (Luton) and 11A (Chalton) after the crash, which took place at around 8.45pm. Initially, National Highways closed junctions 11 to 12 on the southbound carriageway, but this has been revised.

National Highways believes an HGV has 'overturned'. It said in its update: "One of the HGVs involved has overturned and come to rest on its side. There is also significant damage to the nearside barrier and boundary fencing, along with a substantial oil spillage across most lanes.

"Traffic that was caught within the closure has now been released past the scene via lane 4.

"Bedfordshire Police and other emergency services remain in attendance. National Highways Traffic Officers are also on scene assisting with traffic management.

"The carriageway will remain closed while emergency services complete their response, followed by vehicle recovery, barrier repairs and carriageway clean-up."

The incident took place only a few miles from Luton Airport, which is open as normal. A diversion has been created for motorists as the motorway is expected to be closed for some time.

News.title: France wildfires live: 184 arsonists arrested as 'all regions' at risk of further fires
News.content:
Flames are nearing the French Atlantic Coast with raging wildfires now nine miles from Bordeaux as the city's mayor says he's prepared for 'all eventualities'

All regions of France are potentially at risk of wildfires tomorrow as the country grapples with what President Macron has claimed is the "most difficult situation" his country has dealt with since World War Two.

“We are facing two particularly critical days, with the heatwave and the very dry forest,” Gironde mayor Blandine Sarrazin. told local media. "This is the third fire to start here in the last two and a half days, it's really difficult," she added, telling residents it was not yet safe to return home.

Holidaymakers have been forced to leave campsites, tourist homes, holiday villages and leisure parks around Lacanau, which is around 40 miles from Bordeaux. The order comes as firefighters race against time to bring the fires under control before the country's south-west is blasted by a forecast 40C heatwave tomorrow (Wednesday).

Officials say the largest blaze has "stabilised" but have warned it could still burn out of control again as temperatures rise and humidity falls.

But a number of additional fires continue to burn with no end in sight, as local officials warn that the inferno could continue for months before it is fully contained.

France's Interior Minister Laurent Nunez claimed wildfire season is "far from over," and said authorities have arrested 1 84 suspected arsonists since the start of the summer.

Meanwhile in Spain, 63,000 people have been evacuate from their homes near Madrid, with the country's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez calling it "the most painful expression of the climate emergency".

News.title: Tragedy as boy, 15, crushed to death by falling tree during hike at holiday camp
News.content:
Tragedy as boy, 15, crushed to death by falling tree during hike at holiday camp

A teenage boy has tragically died after an incident at YMCA Camp Widjiwagan near Nashville, Tennessee, - the 15-year-old's death has been reproted as 'accidental'

View 3 Images Camden Robert Callihan, and a friend walked under the tree, the friend touched it in a pull-up motion, causing it to fall on Callihan

A 15-year-old boy has tragically died after a tree fell on top of him while out on a walk during holiday camp.

‌



The horror incident happened on July 27 when when two staff at YMCA Camp Widjiwagan in Antioch were “leading campers on a hike when they came across a tree that had fallen and was leaning against another tree above the trail,” police added.

‌



The victim has been identified as Camden Robert Callihan, a camper at YMCA Camp Widjiwagan, the Metropolitan Nashville Police Department said in a release regarding the Monday, July 27, incident.

‌



View 3 Images The entrance to the park

Terrifying wildfire map shows UK towns and cities that would be hit the hardest READ MORE :

The staff instructed the kids “not to touch the tree as they walked under it,” but investigators “were told that as the victim, Camden Robert Callihan, and a friend walked under the tree, the friend touched it in a pull-up motion, causing it to fall on Callihan.”

He was then taken to Vanderbilt University Medical Center, but sadly despite all best efforts he died, the department added. Police have classified Callihan’s death as accidental.

‌



On July 27 the police statement read: "Today's death of a 15-year-old who was fatally injured while on a trail at Camp Widjiwagan is classified as accidental.

View 3 Images A 15-year-old boy died after a tree fell on top of him while on a camp hike in Tennessee, authorities said.

"Two Counselors were leading campers on a hike when they came across a tree that had fallen and was leaning against another tree above the trail. A counselor reported warning the campers not to touch the tree as they walked under it.

Article continues below

Detectives were told that as the victim, Camden Robert Callihan, and a friend walked under the tree, the friend touched it in a pull-up motion, causing it to fall on Callihan.

"The two counselors and other campers lifted the tree off the victim. Emergency care was administered by camp staff. Callihan was rushed by ambulance to Vanderbilt where he died shortly after arrival."

The Mirror has contacted YMCA Camp Widjiwagan for comment but at the time of writing has received no response.

News.content:
Yesterday's final of Love Island crowned Lorenzo and Julia as the 13th season's winners, with Jasmine and Kavan coming second, and Simba and Angelista in third

Love Island final LIVE: Jasmine 'horrified' as she learns public's nickname for her and Lorenzo

The Love Island has officially ended with Lorenzo Alessi and Julia Majchrzak announced as winners, beating out stiff competition from Kavan Murphy and Jasmine Muller.

However, it wasn't without drama as one Islander was noticeably absent from the proceedings, while fans were convinced that there was drama brewing between others.

News.title: Husband finds five dead babies in cardboard boxes 'after argument with wife'
News.content:
Husband finds five dead babies in cardboard boxes 'after argument with wife'

The couple had been arguing over what was in the boxes just a day after the wife gave birth following a pregnancy she denied - the couple have three living children

View 3 Images Five bodies of dead babies have been found at a couple's home (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

A man has found the remains of five babies stuffed into cardboard boxes.

‌



The horrific discoveries were made at a house in France's Provence region on Monday, July 29. The man and his wife cannot be named for legal reasons.

‌



The couple had been arguing over what was in the boxes just a day after giving birth following a pregnancy she denied. This was the the third time she had denied being pregnant, according to media reports.

‌



View 3 Images The entrance of an apartment here five deceased babies were found (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

The woman began suffering from abdominal pains and went to hospital while her husband stayed behind.

According to reports from the Daily Mail, a source said the man "looked inside the cardboard boxes they had been arguing over – that's when he found the five dead babies".

‌



The source said they were all "decomposing, and had been around for quite a while".

The husband notified police who are now investigating the incident.

The couple have three living children, aged eight, twelve and the newborn.

‌



Medical examinations will determine the exact nature of the remains, as well as the circumstances and date of their deaths, with the first forensic examinations, including autopsies carried out today (Wednesday, July 29).

View 3 Images French police seals affixed to the door of an apartment (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

No arrests have been made connection with the case.

‌



The case has drawn parallels to several other newborn murder cases in the country.

In March, a French court jailed a 44-year-old woman for 25 years over the deaths of two of her newborn babies, who police found in the family freezer.

In 2018, a court sentenced a woman to eight years in prison for drowning five of her new-born babies and freezing their bodies.

Article continues below

In 2015, a 45-year-old nursing assistant from northern France confessed to killing her eight newborns at birth and hiding their bodies. The murders were committed between 1989 and 2006, by suffocating eight of her children shortly after giving birth.

News.title: Burnham invites Tories and Lib Dems to social care talks
News.content:
Andy Burnham has invited the leaders of the Conservatives and the Liberal Democrats for talks on reforming social care in England.

The prime minister wants to meet Kemi Badenoch and Sir Ed Davey on Wednesday, when he is expected to give a speech saying that finding cross-party common ground will be key to the reform.

Liberal Dem leader Sir Ed said he would attend remotely but Tory leader Badenoch cannot be there and is sending shadow health secretary Stuart Andrew instead.

A Conservative source criticised the short notice invitation, suggesting: "It's almost like it's only being done for show."

Burnham did not invite the leaders of Reform UK or the Green Party of England and Wales.

Last week the prime minister told the BBC the NHS would "collapse" if social care was not reformed, saying he would not want to leave office without bringing in "substantial change" to the system.

The prime minister said he would put "whatever political capital" he had "into fixing broken social care" but did not put a timeline on changes.

Burnham first proposed a universal system of social care in England in 2009 when he was health secretary under former Prime Minister Gordon Brown.

He suggested a compulsory levy to fund the system and Brown's government also floated the idea of allowing people to defer the payment until after they died, leading to the Tories branding it a "death tax".

In his speech on Wednesday, Burnham is not expected to set out detailed plans for a new system of social care in England.

But the BBC has been told he will announce he is speeding up the Casey Commission, an independent review led by Baroness Louise Casey which will draw up recommendations to deliver a National Care Service.

At the speech, he will be joined by Health Secretary Yvette Cooper. Baroness Casey herself will also be there to launch a consultation that will give the public a chance to share their views on social care.

Speaking ahead of his speech, Burnham said it was "time to draw a line under people playing politics" with social care.

"Last week I said we needed a different kind of politics: problem-solving, not point-scoring," he said.

"Nowhere is that more urgent than social care. For decades, governments have kicked this issue down the road because they've seen it as too risky, too difficult, and too complicated.

"Politicians might have different views but I'm serious about fixing this issue and to do that, we have to find common ground and listen to others to find a way forward."

News.title: Four women accuse Jared Leto of criminal sexual conduct when they were teenagers
News.content:
Warning: Contains graphic details of alleged sexual offences and misconduct, as well as strong language

Four women have accused Oscar-winning actor and Thirty Seconds to Mars frontman Jared Leto of criminal sexual conduct, with the alleged offences having taken place when they were teenagers.

One of the women says she was sexually assaulted in a motel bathroom when she was 17. Another says the Hollywood star threatened her with sexual assault when she was 19, and had been unexpectedly left alone with him in a hotel room.

A third describes how she had under-age sex with the star in California when she was 17 - which would be classified as statutory rape. Leto "shrugged off" a conversation about the age of consent being 18 in the US state, she says.

The fourth woman describes being groomed by Leto, saying he abused his celebrity status by making repeated sexually explicit phone calls to her when she was 16. On at least one occasion, she says he suggested they should have sex.

She was subsequently sent a non-disclosure agreement (NDA) to prevent her from talking about her relationship with Leto, which the BBC has seen. However, she refused to sign.

Four further women also say they received strange and often very sexual phone calls from Leto when they were younger.

Another woman says, when she was 14, he instructed a security guard to take her backstage at a music festival after having made a lewd comment about her chest during an autograph-signing. The girl's mother confronted Leto, but he repeated the comment, it is alleged.

In total, 10 women have spoken to the BBC documentary - Jared Leto: Hollywood's Dark Secret - with nine of them sharing their stories publicly for the first time.

All the women say they encountered Leto between 2002 and 2016, when he was in his 30s and 40s. He is now 54.

"This was 25 years agoâ¦ he has gotten away with it," says one of his alleged victims.

The BBC has corroborated a number of the women's accounts with friends and family who were told about the encounters with Leto at the time. In some cases, we have also seen pictures and messages that support the women's accounts.

Two men who worked with Leto's band for many years also told the documentary how uncomfortable staff felt about the way Leto would interact with teenage girls, sometimes inviting them backstage to his dressing room or inviting them to the house where he was recording.

"I think everyone thought the age gap was way too big," one says.

Despite repeated attempts to contact Jared Leto, he has not responded to the allegations put to him by the BBC.

News.title: Polanski says guillotine re-post was mistake but refuses to apologise
News.content:
Zack Polanski has refused three times to apologise to Nigel Farage for re-posting a photo of a man wearing a t-shirt with an image of a guillotine and the slogan "we're only making plans for Nigel".

Reform UK's home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf, said the image showed a "photo of man calling for the beheading of Nigel Farage", which he said could be an "incitement to murder".

The Green Party of England and Wales leader was reported to the Met over the photo, which he then deleted, but told the BBC he had not been contacted by police.

Speaking to BBC Newsnight, he said he would not apologise for an "inadvertent mistake" that he said Farage had amplified in a "fundamentally dishonest way".

The row kicked off on Monday evening when Polanski shared the photo, which he said was the fifth image in a series of 20 from a party, having accepted a request to collaborate with the Instagram account of a photographer at the event.

Posting a screenshot on X, Reform UK leader Farage said: "If I was to post anything as inciteful then I would expect to be arrested, and so should Polanski."

Asked if he wanted to apologise to Farage, Polanski said: "Well, if I'd done it deliberately I'd be apologising but because this was a mistake I think the important thing is that I point out this was a mistake, that I also make sure that I condemn political violence, and also crucially I make a commitment to be better on social media."

Asked for a second time whether he would apologise, Polanski refused because he said Farage had cropped the image to make it look like he had posted it himself, which he said was "fundamentally dishonest" and only amplified the problem.

Saying he had received a death threat earlier on Tuesday, Polanski added: "The ramping up of the language to say 'this is incitement to murder me' feels like that's also putting me in a dangerous spot."

Given a third chance to apologise, Polanski doubled down and said: "You know as well as I do that as soon as I do that Nigel Farage would run all over social media saying he was correct about incitement to murder and this would all ramp up again.

"I think it's important that I draw a line and don't play his game... It is important that he's kept safe, it is important we condemn political violence, but I also recognise this as the political attack that it is."

"If Nigel Farage wants to apologise for all the times that he's put other people in danger then I will be happy to make an apology," Polanski added.

The Green leader explained he had not read the slogan on the T-shirt when he accepted the collaboration because "what I was seeing was people partying" and he only noticed the man was wearing a rainbow hat as he flicked through.

"It feels quite surreal to be having this conversation," he said, adding: "I think it would be odd for the police to speak to me about that because I think it's quite obvious I've not done anything wrong other than make an inadvertent mistake."

The Metropolitan Police said there was no update on the complaint they had received on Monday.

On Tuesday, Reform asked the monitoring officer from the Greater London Authority, where Polanski is an elected member, to investigate whether he had breached the code of conduct.

Keith Prince, a Reform London Assembly Member, said: "To say that he was unaware of what he was promoting is frankly risible."

A Reform UK source told BBC Newsnight: "It's truly astonishing and quite frankly sickening that Zack Polanski won't apologise for inciting murder.

"He admits it was wrong. He admits it's dangerous, but he still refuses to apologise. Mr Polanski is not fit to lead a national political party."

Asked about the row on Tuesday, Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden said there was a "duty on all politicians to be careful about what they post", especially in light of the death of former MP Ann Widdecombe earlier this month.

News.title: The evidence that shows today's 20-somethings really do have it worse
News.content:
Young people in their 20s are facing a tougher start to adulthood than any generation in almost half a century, according to analysis of UK data on housing, employment and wealth, carried out for the BBC.

More than 40% of 25-year-olds are now living with their parents, their wages have stagnated and employment has fallen, show the figures which compare key metrics for different generations at age 25 stretching back to the early 1980s.

The findings are underscored by the experiences of young people themselves who, along with parents, have contacted BBC Your Voice about their circumstances, with many saying they were frustrated about being accused by older generations of not trying hard enough.

We asked the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) to gather and analyse government data, external, for the first time, to see if this generation really does have it worse.

The biggest change it found was where those in their 20s are living.

News.title: 'No safe options' for thousands sheltering in key Sudan city as RSF fighters advance
News.content:
Thousands of people who have poured into the city of el-Obeid hoping to find shelter from Sudan's raging civil war have found themselves under threat again, amid warnings that paramilitary fighters are preparing to descend on the army-controlled city.

Clashes between the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the military has escalated in the North Kordofan region - a critical target for both sides in the conflict which could open a gateway into contested territory.

Displaced people have flocked to el-Obeid, which remains heavily defended by the Sudanese military, despite ongoing strikes being carried out on the city as paramilitary forces advance. The UN's International Organization for Migration (IOM) said it has become a key refuge for people escaping ongoing violence in the surrounding areas.

Satellite imagery shows the main displacement camp has expanded significantly since March, with aid workers reporting dozens of new arrivals each day.

"Families have run out of safe options to protect themselves," Mohamed Refaat, IOM chief of mission in Sudan, said. "Many have already been displaced before and are once again forced to leave behind their homes, livelihoods and support networks."

The UN and G7 foreign ministers have now issued warnings that the RSF may be preparing to attack the city, raising fears that atrocities akin to those seen during the massacre in el-Fasher could be repeated. Thousands of people were killed in mass executions after the paramilitary overran SAF troops defending the city last October, in one of the worst atrocities since the civil war began in 2023.

Fears of similar reprisals occurring in el-Obeid have grown for weeks and verified footage now shows dozens of heavily armed RSF troops in armoured trucks stationed in Nyala, a key nearby stronghold, vowing to "liberate" the city.

News.title: Report on Jewish diaspora finds biggest rise in antisemitism in UK
News.content:
The UK recorded the biggest rise in antisemitic incidents last year of any country with a major Jewish population outside Israel, according to a new report.

Published by the J7 Large Communities' Task Force Against Antisemitism, the report also found that 2025 had been the deadliest year for Jews living outside Israel in more than three decades.

The task force is a group of organisations representing the seven largest Jewish diaspora communities.

It found that antisemitism in Argentina, Australia, Canada, France, Germany, the UK and the US â which together are home to more than 90% of the world's Jewish population outside Israel â remained at record levels.

Reported antisemitic incidents across the seven countries have risen by 136% since 2022, the year before the Hamas attacks on southern Israel and the start of the war in Gaza, while violent incidents have risen by 97%.

The UK was one of only three countries where reported antisemitic incidents increased in 2025, alongside Argentina and Germany. Incidents recorded in the UK rose by 5% compared with the previous year â the largest increase among the seven countries.

Although reported incidents fell in 2025 in the US, Australia, Canada and France compared with 2024, every country remained significantly above levels before 7 October 2023.

In 2025, 20 people were killed in antisemitic attacks, the highest annual death toll since the bombing of a Jewish community centre in the Argentinian capital Buenos Aires in 1994.

News.title: Brits urged to avoid dangerous plug adaptors this summer - what to watch out for
News.content:
Brits going on holiday abroad this summer have been warned to watch out for dangerous travel adaptors, after an investigation suggested thousands may be for sale online.

Consumer safety group Electrical Safety First (ESF) tested 14 products from AliExpress, Amazon Marketplace, eBay and TikTok Shop - and found they all failed to meet UK safety requirements.

It said in some instances the devices could expose users to risk of serious electric shock or electrocution.

AliExpress, Amazon, eBay and TikTok all said they had removed the products ESF flagged from sale, and that they treated product safety as a top priority.

But Giuseppe Capanna, ESF product safety engineer, urged those "heading abroad this summer to think before they buy".

"What looks like a bargain could come at a much higher cost," he warned.

Capanna also said shoppers should buy travel adaptors from trusted retailers "so they can travel with confidence".

ESF tested six regular travel adaptors and eight universal adaptors it suspected could pose safety concerns.

To be sold in the UK, adaptors must not have accessible live parts and only one set of pins should come out at a time.

But the charity found multiple sets could be exposed simultaneously in six out of eight of the universal adaptors it tested.

None of the eight met the required dimensions and mechanical strength, while some pins snapped off under force during tests.

ESF said anyone who tried to remove a broken pin from a socket would be at risk of electric shock.

News.title: Amber heat health alerts to come into force as heatwave reaches 35C peak
News.content:
Amber and yellow heat health alerts are set to come into force on Wednesday as parts of the UK endure the fourth widespread heatwave of the year so far.

Temperatures are forecast to peak at midweek with readings as high as 35C (95F) in the hottest places.

Though the heatwave will come to a quick end for many on Thursday, well above-average temperatures in the mid- to high 20s Celsius will persist into the weekend.

The hot weather, paired with a significant lack of rainfall, will exacerbate conditions in many of the driest areas.

News.title: Burnham has no scope to increase borrowing, think tank warns
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham will have to raise taxes or cut spending to meet his pledges on defence and the cost of living, a major think tank has said.

Burnham has announced a series of new measures since assuming office last week, including cuts to electricity bills and bringing the bus fare cap in most parts of England back down to Â£2.

But the National Institute of Economic and Social Research (Niesr) warned the public finances will continue to be squeezed by more persistent inflation as a result of the Iran war.

It questioned whether Burnham had "fully thought through" how his promises would be paid for, but said the prime minister will have to raise taxes or cut spending elsewhere.

Stephen Millard, Niesr's deputy director for macroeconomics, said: "There's clearly no scope for increasing borrowing, so it is about choices."

Labour's manifesto pledge was to not increase taxes for working people - including income tax, VAT and national insurance contributions - which Burnham has said he will uphold.

Millard said Niesr was advocating for cost-of-living measures to be funded through higher taxes â "which could involve tax reform rather than higher marginal rates" â or spending cuts.

He said: "People have talked a lot about the welfare bill â that is an obvious place to look.

"The triple lock on pensions, that is very, very expensive, and will get more expensive as we age."

He also pointed to potentially reforming council tax to move towards a land value tax system, or scrapping some VAT exemptions.

"Once you've done all of that, then I'm afraid I would break the manifesto promise and would be looking at the income tax rate."

Niesr also said on Wednesday it expects inflation to keep rising until February 2027, peaking at 3.8% before falling back to the Bank of England's 2% target.

The think tank said in its latest economic outlook that it does not believe the central bank will cut interest rates until 2028.

Its Director David Aikman said that "treading water is not enough" to prevent the national debt from rising.

"Every major shock this century has ratcheted the debt ratio higher, and none of that increase has been reversed," he said.

The Treasury said the government will stick to its fiscal rules while investing in "the public services people rely on".

"Fiscal discipline is the bedrock of economic stability and national security," a spokesperson said.

News.title: French Navy carries out 'shooting drill' mid interview
News.content:
A French Navy patrol boat appeared to fire a round of gunshots "without warning" in the English Channel during a BBC interview with the UK shadow home secretary.

Conservative MP Chris Philp was being interviewed about small boat crossings by BBC journalist Michael Keohan as a French warship passed by at 09:15 BST (10:15 CET), about three miles from the French coast.

Keohan said there were 17 shots but "no warnings" from the boat about 300m away, which left Philp believing it was an intimidation tactic to "stop us covering migrant crossings".

The French authorities said it was part of a training exercise, unrelated to the presence of a British ship, which it said was out of range of fire.

Philp dismissed this claim as "not credible", adding: "There were no warnings in place about live firing training exercises.

"It looked and sounded exactly like deliberate intimidation."

News.title: Grieving mum was told baby's ashes were animal remains
News.content:
Ness suffered a miscarriage just before she was due to have her 12-week scan on April 20 2021.

She told how she had treasured the ashes for three years.

"They had sat on my shelf next to my baby scan," said Ness.

In court, prosecutor Chris Paxton KC said "the ashes that Lucy was given could not have been those of her baby".

The barrister did not state that they were of animal origin.

Ness was clear to the BBC, however, that police had told her the ashes were animal remains.

Her disgust at Bush was clear.

She said: "How can somebody with a duty of care do this to my family?"

She and her partner, Callum Ellerby, were told their baby was cremated on 10 May 2021.

"We didn't know the gender," said Ness. "We were not going to know the gender."

The day after the cremation was meant to have taken place, Bush, from Legacy Independent Funeral Directors, rang her and asked her to collect the ashes, which she did.

They were contained in a white china urn with a teddy bear embossed on it, Ness recalled.

When Humberside Police announced they were investigating Legacy in March 2024, Ness rang the helpline set up for anyone concerned.

The force then contacted her to say the ashes she had in her home could not be that of her baby, she said.

Officers explained to Ness that they had checked records at the crematorium and found Bush collected the baby's ashes on 13 May - two days after he had presented Ness and Ellerby with the urn.

She said: "I have felt very up and down. This has definitely impacted on my mental health."

News.title: Some parents on benefits to get up to £4,500 for child starting apprenticeship
News.content:
Some parents on benefits will be given up to Â£4,500 a year to encourage their children to start apprenticeships, the government has said.

Under plans to encourage young people into work, families will be offered a bursary to replace Universal Credit payments lost by starting jobs.

The payment is expected to benefit an estimated few thousand households, who currently face losing between Â£17 and Â£330 a week if their children start apprenticeships.

The Conservatives welcomed Prime Minister Andy Burnham's support for apprenticeships, but criticised his plans to fund the bursaries.

The bursary will be paid for from a Â£30m pot, funded through the growth and skills levy, a tax on employers with annual wage bills over Â£3m.

It followed the publication of a Social Security Advisory Committee report, external which warned of the "perverse effects" of the benefits system on young people's employment choices.

It said, for example, single parents with a disabled child could lose up to Â£340 per week in benefits if their child started an apprenticeship, exceeding the expected apprenticeship salary of Â£258 per week.

Because they are classed as paid employment, benefit payments are reduced to households where young people take on apprenticeships.

The committee said the system was hampering government efforts to reduce the number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet).

In a recent report, former Health Secretary Alan Milburn warned that one in six young people could be Neet in the next five years unless urgent action is taken.

Official figures show more than a million people aged 16 to 24 are currently Neet.

The government said its new bursary would remove a barrier to young people taking on apprenticeships, allowing them to "earn and learn".

Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden said: "By providing bursaries to those who need them most and fully funding apprenticeship training, we are making sure cost is not the reason someone misses out."

It is part of a wider package of support for apprenticeships, including funding for apprenticeship training for under-25s and additional support for employers taking on apprentices.

Helen Whately, the Shadow Work and Pensions Secretary, said: "I'm glad Burnham agrees: apprenticeships are a good thing, and we need more of them."

But she said the plan was "uncosted".

"It is spending money already committed elsewhere. So, either it is another unfunded announcement, or Andy Burnham is not being straight with us about his plans."

Burnham has said he is "on a mission" to reduce the number of Neets.

"The trend is rising at the moment, so the first thing I've got to do is to stop that rise," he said.

As he continues a flurry of early policy announcements, Burnham on Tuesday set out plans to strike a balance in the education system between prioritising academic and technical skills.

News.title: Naga Munchetty to leave BBC Breakfast after 17 years
News.content:
Munchetty, 51, is among the best-paid presenters on the BBC's star salaries list, earning about Â£360,000 a year, according to the latest accounts.

She has interviewed major celebrities and politicians on the programme over the years ranging from Hillary Clinton and Michelle Obama to Sir Keir Starmer, Sir David Attenborough and Sir Rod Stewart.

In 2016, she appeared on the BBC's Strictly Come Dancing.

She has also been at the centre of some controversies during her time on BBC Breakfast.

In 2019, she was initially found to have breached the BBC's guidelines over comments she made about a social media post from Donald Trump about four female politicians of colour.

However, the BBC's director general then reversed that finding after deciding her words were not "sufficient to merit" upholding part of the complaint.

In 2021, Munchetty and co-presenter Charlie Stayt were "spoken to and reminded of their responsibilities" after complaints about their reaction to a government minister's flag. Munchetty apologised for liking "offensive" tweets about the exchange.

In June 2025, the Sun reported details of two alleged incidents which the paper said caused BBC bosses to speak to Munchetty about her conduct.

That came amid reports of behind-the-scenes tensions on the show, and at the same time as the programme's editor Richard Frediani took extended leave following allegations about his behaviour.

Frediani returned to work two weeks later and remains editor of BBC Breakfast.

At the time, the BBC said it did not comment on individual cases but took all complaints about conduct at work extremely seriously. Munchetty and Frediani did not comment on the reports.

The programme won a Bafta TV Award last year for best news coverage for a special about the Post Office scandal.

News.title: Laughter and tears at Dame Penelope Keith funeral
News.content:
Dame Penelope Keith's funeral has been hailed as "wonderful, beautiful and absolutely amazing" by her friends.

The actress, who starred in The Good Life and To The Manor Born, "died peacefully whilst living with cancer at her home" on 29 June at the age of 86.

Crowds lined the streets to say their goodbyes to the "very special lady" as her coffin travelled through her home town of Milford in Surrey before the service at Guildford Cathedral.

Broadcaster, writer and former politician Gyles Brandreth said the funeral was "filled with a mixture of sadness but laughter and gratitude as well because we were celebrating a great actress".

"It was a wonderful way to remember a remarkable person," he told BBC Radio Surrey.

Posting on X later, he said: "There was laughter and tears at Guildford Cathedral this morning - a truly beautiful and deeply moving funeral service for Dame Penelope Keith - what a lady and what a perfect service.

"It caught her completely. She was very special."

News.title: Unsolved Suzy Lamplugh case 'haunts' detectives
News.content:
Police officers investigating the disappearance of estate agent Suzy Lamplugh in west London say they remain "haunted" by the case, four decades after she went missing.

Lamplugh, 25, vanished after leaving her Fulham office to meet a client on the afternoon of 28 July 1986. She never returned and her body has never been found.

As the Metropolitan Police investigation is due to be mothballed next year, cold case detectives say they are troubled by the continuing mystery.

To mark the 40th anniversary of her disappearance, the Lamplugh family has released previously unseen photographs featuring her siblings Lizzie, Tamsin and Richard and her parents Paul and Diana.

In releasing the intimate family images, her siblings described her as "a truly beautiful person inside and out".

News.title: Two-Michelin-star chef brings fine dining to town football club
News.content:
Football fans will have the chance to swap their traditional match day pint and pie for a pop-up dining experience created by a renowned two-Michelin-star chef.

Gareth Ward, the chef behind Ynyshir Restaurant and Rooms near Machynlleth, Powys - which has an almost Â£500 per head tasting menu - has partnered up with Aberystwyth Town Football Club, in Ceredigion.

The collaboration will bring supporters different match day dining experiences, hospitality packages and corporate events throughout the season.

Ward, who has featured as a guest judge on MasterChef: The Professionals, said he was "excited" for the new venture.

The chef-patron said football clubs should be at "the heart of their communities".

The club's team is in the Novira Cymru South division, the second tier of Welsh football.

He added: "I see a real opportunity to bring people together through food and unforgettable matchday experiences and corporate events."

At least 30 people were killed reportedly in police firing in Pakistan-administered Kashmir as parts of the region went to the polls amid heavy security.

According to the Awami Action Committee (JAAC), at least 25 people were killed on Monday and five more on Tuesday as the police fired at the supporters of the banned civil rights group, reported the Guardian.

Imtiaz Aslam, a core member of the JAAC, had earlier claimed in a video that several of its supporters died in clashes with the police.

open image in gallery People gather near closed shops at a marketplace in Muzaffarabad, the capital of Pakistan-administered Kashmir on 16 June 2026 amid protests called by the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) ( AFP/Getty )

“Today, the forces from Pakistan opened fire on our innocent youths. As a result, 14 of our young people have been martyred. Among them is Usman Nazir, the younger brother of the movement’s founder, Omar Nazir Kashmiri.

“Other martyrs include a companion from Khaigala, one from Kotli city, one from Tattapani, one from Banja-Baspoor, one from Chhota Gala, and one from Haveli.

open image in gallery Pakistan Frontier Constabulary personnel stand guard along a street in Muzaffarabad, the capital of Pakistan-administered Kashmir on 26 July 2026 on the eve of the first phase of the regional elections ( AFP/Getty )

“In total, 14 have been martyred, including two of our Baloch friends. Almost two dozen others are injured,” he had said earlier.

Spokesperson for JAAC, SA Khan, alleged that Pakistan’s security agencies fired at unarmed protesters in Mirpur on Tuesday and then took away the “dead bodies” to remove the proof.

“We have the photos and video evidence of dead bodies lying on streets in a pool of blood. The security forces abducted the dead bodies to erase the evidence.”

The Independent has reached out to Pakistan’s prime minister’s office for comment.

Amnesty International demanded a “prompt, independent and transparent investigation” in the allegations of the use of force by security forces against protesters. The human rights body also demanded the restoration of internet on the ground.

The organisation’s acting regional director for South Asia, Isabelle Lassee, said: “We urge the Pakistani authorities to restore all communications access and allow media and independent observers into the area.”

“Tensions around this election are being heightened by the unlawful ban on the Jammu and Kashmir Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC). Amnesty International has repeatedly called on the Pakistani authorities to lift the ban on this protest movement and stop weaponising anti-terror laws to silence and arbitrarily detain JAAC members and supporters. The ban cannot be used as an excuse to mete out deadly violence against protesters.”

While Pakistani authorities have rejected the accusation of killing civilian protesters, information minister, Atta Tarar, accused India of financing the protests in the region.

Rejecting the allegation, Mr Khan said: “It is nothing new: people asking for political or economic rights are termed India-sponsored or anti-state in Pakistan, same goes in India.”

Founded in 2023, the JAAC is a grassroots coalition of businessmen, students, and civil society activists that has demanded subsidised food prices for the locals.

The alliance had been staging sit-ins at multiple locations since last month, demanding the abolition of 12 of the 53 seats in the regional legislative assembly reserved for refugees who migrated to Pakistan from Indian-administered Kashmir decades ago.

The group argues the reserved seats give disproportionate political influence to people who live outside the territory.

The dispute escalated in early June after the regional Supreme Court ruled that the refugee seats are protected and cannot be abolished without a constitutional amendment.

The seats were created to represent people displaced from Indian-administered Kashmir by the decades-old dispute over the Himalayan region.

India and Pakistan each administer part of Kashmir but claim the territory in its entirety. The nuclear-armed neighbours have fought two of their three wars over Kashmir since gaining independence from British rule in 1947.

open image in gallery A woman casts her ballot at a polling station during the first phase of regional elections in Pakistan-administered Kashmir's Mirpur on 27 July 2026 ( AFP/Getty )

The clashes in the region are the latest in the spate of violence erupting in the region, as the group clashed with the security forces in the region.

Earlier, on 14 July, at least nine people were killed and several wounded in clashes that erupted after Pakistani authorities reopened roads that followers of the banned JAAC had blocked for nearly a month.

Residents have complained of food and medicine shortages as well as restricted transport due to the group’s blockade, according to a police statement.

Polling, originally scheduled for a single day, will now take place in three phases, with first phase of voting completed on 27 July.

The other two phases are scheduled for 2 August and 10 August. The revision of dates came amid concerns over stretched security personnel, reported Al Jazeera.

About 40 people have been killed in poll violence since early June of which 34 were protesters and remaining six were police and paramilitary forces, reported the BBC. The violence has prompted authorities to suspend mobile and internet services across most of the territory.

“The internet shutdown has created serious difficulties … for political candidates and the electoral process itself. Reaching voters has become much harder,” Malik Alauddin, an independent candidate, told the AFP.

“If the internet were available, a single social media post could reach thousands of voters, but now we have to travel to every small village,” he said.

Mahasen Faqih and her husband returned this week to their village in southern Lebanon, digging through the debris of their home in search of their belongings, as part of the U.S.-brokered “pilot zones” agreement in which Israel agreed to withdraw in exchange for the disarmament of the Iran-backed Hezbollah militant group.

The couple fled north shortly after the start of the latest Israel-Hezbollah war, in early March. Now, their home in Zawtar al-Gharbieh — one of three zones where Israel agreed to turn over control to the Lebanese army — is among homes so damaged that they're unlivable. But Faqih said they've vowed to stay, settling inside the large grocery shop that they own in the village as they wait to have their home demolished and rebuilt.

“Zawtar is our small homeland, and we are very happy,” Faqih, 58, said. “We will sleep here to tell the Israelis that we will stay in our land and will not leave it, no matter what happens.”

A week after the Lebanese army took control, only about 15 families have returned, according to Mayor Abed Ezzeldine, who says nearly half the village’s 500 homes have been destroyed and many others damaged.

Hezbollah is strongly opposed to the initial deal reached between Israel and Lebanon — which remain technically in a state of war since Israel’s establishment in 1948 — and to the direct talks between the nations, ongoing for nearly three months.

The latest Israel-Hezbollah war began March 2, when the Lebanese militant group fired rockets into Israel two days after Israel and the U.S. launched their war on Iran. Israel has since invaded Lebanon and occupied dozens of villages in the south along its border.

Under the deal, Israeli forces are supposed to withdraw from some occupied areas of southern Lebanon. But the location of the initial pilot zones generated some controversy in Lebanon. Israeli troops weren't present in most of the areas, raising questions about how a withdrawal could happen. In Zawtar al-Gharbieh, it's unclear whether troops were on the ground. But they were in adjacent areas, and the village was under heavy fire, preventing civilian residents and the Lebanese army from entering until last week.

The Israeli military has destroyed 24 centuries-old villages and 15,000 to 20,000 houses in Lebanon, Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz told a TV station Tuesday. He said Israeli troops control 700 square kilometers (270 square miles) of southern Lebanon and “are preventing raids on the communities.”

Residents return to damaged or destroyed homes in Zawtar al-Gharbieh

On Tuesday, as Faqih sifted through debris, she was able to recover only nine plates from the kitchen. That room and the main sitting room were knocked out, with the ceiling partially collapsed. On the home's other side, an Israeli strike left a hole in the main bedroom's ceiling.

“We are gathering what remains of what we have collected over 45 years,” Faqih said, noting that she'd already sold $20,000 in jewelry to repair the home from damage in the 2024 Israel-Hezbollah war — something she can no longer afford. She hopes the government will help them rebuild.

Mayor Ezzeldine said Zawtar al-Gharbieh is "disaster-stricken.”

“You can see some homes standing, but they are not suitable for living and cannot be renovated,” he said. The municipality is doing its best to bring water by tanker trucks to residents who return, he said, and he hopes about 100 families will be in the village by week's end.

Lebanese army bulldozers were clearing debris from the village's streets. In the main square, trucks with mounted machine guns were parked near a partially destroyed blue-domed mosque. About 100 meters (109 yards) away, an armored personnel carrier blocked a road leading to the adjacent village of Zawtar al-Sharqiyah, which is fully occupied by Israeli troops.

During The Associated Press team's visit Tuesday to Zawtar al-Gharbieh, three strong explosions occurred in occupied areas, and brown smoke billowed.

More Lebanon-Israel talks are scheduled next month

In his comments Tuesday to Channel 14, an ultranationalist station in Israel, Defense Minister Katz said that in the 24 villages destroyed in Lebanon, “there were Shiites who acted as enemies on behalf of Hezbollah and threatened our borders, our residents, and constantly carried out provocations.”

“Not house by house, not incrimination — all these villages, their destruction has been completed,” he said.

His comments and the return of some residents to the pilot zone come as technical teams from Lebanon and Israel are scheduled to hold another round of talks in Rome over three days starting Aug. 4.

In Beirut, a Lebanese foreign ministry official said the talks will focus on finding other pilot zones to be handed over by Israel's military to the Lebanese side. The official spoke on condition of anonymity in line with regulations.

But in Zawtar al-Gharbieh, mayor Ezzeldine said he wouldn't call the pilot zone successful so far. Israeli troops are still stationed nearby, with drones continuously flying over the village, he said, adding that only the Lebanese army's presence is reassuring residents.

Faqih said that her family does not feel secure and that if Israel expands the pilot zones by a village every couple of months, it will take years “for it to withdraw and for the south to be liberated.”

“We don’t have safety, not even 1%,” she said. “I am not happy with the situation at all.”

______

Associated Press writer Natalie Melzer in Nahariya, Israel, contributed to this report.

Tui River Cruises has floated out its first purpose-built river cruise ship for the Douro.

The new ship, Tui Luzia, was tested on the water for the first time in Kladovo, Serbia.

The finishes touches to the interior and exterior of the vessel are now being completed at the Concordia Damen shipyard

Scheduled for delivery in June 2027, Tui Luzia will spend her inaugural season sailing itineraries on the Douro river in Portugal.

It will be the cruise line’s first time sailing in the region.

The ship will sail a seven-night “Douro Discovery” itinerary from Porto. Highlights include the old stone houses of Entre-os-Rios, a chance to explore almond and olive groves, and a visit to the vineyards of Barca d’Alva.

The ship will accommodate 111 passengers in 56 cabins. Passengers will have access to four decks including a top deck complete with a shallow pool and sun loungers. Cinder, a bar and dining area, will be open every day for drinks and self-serve lunches.

open image in gallery Tui Luzia has been tested on the water and the finishes touches will be added before its 2027 launch ( Tui )

Other venues on the ship include Novo, the main lounge bar, and Retreat, a hybrid area offering a juice bar and an intimate secondary lounge for a quiet evening drink.

Guests will also be able to eat at Sores, the main restaurant serving breakfast through to dinner and Vinha, a Portuguese-inspired al fresco dining space where guests can enjoy a la carte dinner.

Similar to the other Tui River Cruises ships, Tui Luzia will be Full Board Plus as standard.

This covers tea, coffee, soft drinks, wine or beer with meals. Any other drinks need to be paid for, or passengers can upgrade to all inclusive.

Cruise fares start from £1,859 per person. Flight are included.

Katy Berzins, head of river cruises at Tui, said: “The float out of Tui Luzia marks another significant milestone for Tui River Cruises and our longstanding partnership with Concordia Damen.

“As our first purpose-built ship, Tui Luzia represents an exciting new chapter for our brand.”

News.content:

Like so many others, my anxious attachment style reached its unbearable apex during the pandemic. I remember staring at my phone, watching friends typing and sending messages in a WhatsApp group, feeling like I couldn’t breathe. Paranoia told me they were gossiping about me behind my back in a separate group. So I sent messages to each of them individually to make sure everything was okay. Of course, it was. But the noise in my head was not.

People talk about attachment theory a lot. But for the most part, the conversation centres on romantic relationships: is the reason you’re not ready to call him your boyfriend because you’re an avoidant? Are you catastrophising about why she hasn’t replied to your texts because you’re anxious? Do you never worry about anything much at all because you’re a secure unicorn?

But rarely do we look at how attachment theory can be applied to friendships. And yet, it obviously plays an integral role, manifesting in different ways in different friendships. “The way we learned to relate to our earliest caregivers travels with us into every significant relationship we form, including our friendships,” explains Dr Jemma Anderson, an HCPC registered educational psychologist. “Our attachment style shapes what we expect from close relationships, how safe we feel being vulnerable, how we respond when a friend lets us down, and what we do when intimacy starts to feel like too much.”

Like with romantic attachment styles, these aren’t modes of behaviour that we consciously choose; otherwise surely all of us would prefer to be securely attached, whereby you can exhibit healthy conflict resolution, emotional safety, and general stability because of how safe you feel within yourself. Some people might be lucky enough to be this way naturally given their upbringing, but a lot of us, particularly people like me from broken homes, invariably have to learn it the hard way.

open image in gallery Attachment styles are often discussed in relation to romantic relationships – we need to start applying them to friendships ( Getty )

In some cases, one person’s anxious attachment can exacerbate the others within the same dynamic. This was what happened to Maggie*, 30, with her closest friend, Jess, from university. “After we graduated, we would text and voice note every single day, seeing each other every weekend and describing ourselves as a duo,” she recalls.

The dynamic shifted when Maggie made a new friend, Fran, on a cheerleading team in London. “For numerous reasons, Jess didn’t like Fran and pretty much told me that if I was going to be friends with her, then I couldn’t be friends with her too.” For whatever reason, Jess couldn’t overcome the feeling that she’d been replaced, which might’ve stemmed from an anxious attachment friendship style.

Something similar happened with another one of Maggie’s university friends, Sarah. “We were conjoined from our very first day,” she recalls, explaining how they’d walk to lectures together, go on nights out together, and eventually moved to the US together for a year abroad.

Things took a turn when the pair moved in together in London, and Sarah’s anxiety got more severe. “She would get really angry and claim that I was phasing her out,” Maggie remembers. “I would still respond to all of her messages, just not immediately. She started making incessant demands for attention and was always unhappy with me. I just eventually felt like I couldn’t keep up anymore.”

Anxious attachment can stem from growing up in an environment where caregiving felt inconsistent or unpredictable. “You might find yourself analysing a friend’s tone in a message, misreading a slow reply, or feeling disproportionately hurt when plans change,” explains Dr Anderson. “The fear underneath this behaviour is usually that you’re too much or not enough for others.”

This was certainly how I felt in that pandemic-induced panic, though I’d had similar experiences leading up to it: always fearing the worst if a friend didn’t reply to my texts within what felt like a typical timeframe, overthinking the most innocuous of texts, and generally being very paranoid and insecure in my friendships.

The way we learned to relate to our earliest caregivers travels with us into every significant relationship we form, including our friendships Dr Jemma Anderson, HCPC-registered educational psychologist

“Anxiously attached people can give a lot to friendships, sometimes more than feels sustainable, because giving feels like a way of securing the connection,” adds Dr Anderson. “When this level of input isn’t reciprocated, the disappointment and betrayal can feel devastating rather than inconvenient or a little frustrating.”

It can also be hard work for the person on the receiving end, rupturing friendships and causing lasting trauma in the process. This was the case for Yas*, 31, and her friend Emily*. “It feels especially striking when we are planning things,” she says. “There’s a level of detail and confirmation that she tends to need for a plan that I just don’t require at all, and it can turn meeting up into a bit of a palaver. I will enjoy it when we do meet up, obviously, but sometimes the level of admin required to get there can be a little draining.”

This behaviour shows up as neediness, which can be an instant repellent that then brings up a degree of guilt. “I think I’ve noticed it a bit more in the past couple of months as I’ve gone through a breakup which has really impacted my capacity to do all the ordinary life admin things, like keeping up with WhatsApps,” adds Yas. “I know that this all probably comes from a good place, so then I just feel a bit mean for moaning about it.”

open image in gallery ‘I was always fearing the worst if a friend didn’t reply to my texts within what felt like a typical timeframe, overthinking the most innocuous of texts’ ( Alamy/PA )

Avoidance can appear very differently in friendships. From the outside, it may look like hyper-independence. But get closer to an avoidant person, and you’ll quickly realise there are certain barriers they won’t cross. “Deep emotional conversations can feel uncomfortable and the prospect of relying on or needing someone else can feel dangerous,” says Dr Anderson. “Similarly, being relied upon or needed by others can feel equally suffocating and unsafe.”

The final attachment type is disorganised, which is when people recognise both anxious and avoidant traits in themselves. It’s more common than people realise and can be confusing to experience, given the contradictions that can arise. “It can look like wanting closeness desperately while simultaneously pushing it away,” says Dr Anderson. “They might pursue friendship intensely, then feel overwhelmed by the intimacy and resort to withdrawal or crave connection but expect disappointment and resort to sabotage before they can be hurt.”

The good news is that all of this can be remedied through a combination of introspection, self-awareness, and really good therapy. This was what enabled Maggie to push past her own anxiously attached friendships as she moved through her twenties. “If you don’t feel good enough in yourself, that’s not something that you should be inflicting on other people,” she says. “For me it was about learning my self-worth and understanding that if I didn’t say yes to everything, and I didn’t people-please all the time, that people were still gonna like me and want me in their lives.”

Security in friendship isn’t a personality trait you either have or don’t. It builds through accumulated experience of having your needs met, understood and responded to Dr Elena Touroni, consultant psychologist

If you’re unsure of your own attachment style in friendships and feel that you could be something other than secure (like most of us), it’s best to start off by looking for patterns. “Do you assume the worst if a friend goes quiet for a few days?” suggests Lorin Krenn, a relationships coach. “Do you avoid reaching out because you don’t want to be a burden? Once you recognise those patterns, you can begin separating what’s happening now from the fears you’ve carried over from past experiences. That awareness is important because it stops you interpreting every slow reply or cancelled plan as rejection, and it makes it easier to communicate what you actually need from your friendships.”

“Security in friendship isn’t a personality trait you either have or don’t. It builds through accumulated experience of having your needs met, understood and responded to,” adds Dr Elena Touroni, consultant psychologist and co-founder of The Chelsea Psychology Clinic. “Good therapy can help people understand where these patterns originated, but a great deal also shifts through choosing friendships carefully and allowing yourself to be fully known in them.”

It’s worth pushing through. For me, a combination of therapy, honest conversations with friends, and emotional maturity was the key. These days, I’m much better at self-soothing in moments of anxiety; an unreplied text no longer elicits the kind of panic it once did, and I’m on my way to feeling secure.

*Names have been changed

News.title: Why Burnham’s plans for education could limit girls’ horizons
News.content:
Your support helps us to tell the story Read more Support Now From reproductive rights to climate change to Big Tech, The Independent is on the ground when the story is developing. Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging. At such a critical moment in US history, we need reporters on the ground. Your donation allows us to keep sending journalists to speak to both sides of the story. The Independent is trusted by Americans across the entire political spectrum. And unlike many other quality news outlets, we choose not to lock Americans out of our reporting and analysis with paywalls. We believe quality journalism should be available to everyone, paid for by those who can afford it. Your support makes all the difference. Read more

When prime minister Andy Burnham announced this week that schools should adapt their curricula to meet local labour market needs, I understood the instinct. It is clear that we are in danger of losing a generation of young people in the UK and qualifications alone are not enough. We urgently need new ideas, so Burnham’s interventions are a welcome step.

As CEO of Inspiring Girls, I regularly speak to girls aged 11-16 years old and know the issues young people face are myriad, including that girls still face persistent gender stereotypes, confidence gaps and unequal representation in many careers, along with a lack of visible role models.

open image in gallery Burnham’s intervention is welcome – but he must ensure they don’t stifle potential ( Reuters )

Career aspirations are already narrowed by societal conditions. Research from 2024 showed that gender stereotypes have stopped nearly half of girls aged 11 to 18 from doing something they want to do. The confidence gap is even starker. Between the ages of eight and 14, girls’ confidence levels drop by 30 per cent while boys' confidence wavers as well, but the gap that opens at age 12 doesn’t close throughout adolescence.

The mechanism is simple: if girls can’t see it, how can they know they can be it? Girls need to see what is possible

At age 14, girls experience their lowest levels of self-assurance, 27 per cent lower than boys report at the same age. This is the precise moment when career aspirations form and girls are losing faith in themselves exactly when they need it most. Add a curriculum narrowed to what your region happens to need right now, and you risk cementing that inequality rather than breaking it.

At Inspiring Girls International, we work across 40 countries, connecting girls with female role models. The mechanism is simple: if girls can’t see it, how can they know they can be it? Girls need to see what is possible. When we connect them with role models, especially role models from different regions, different backgrounds, different possibilities, something shifts. Suddenly what’s possible expands.

The research on aspirations tells us that they're not formed by geography alone. Research from the OECD found that 47 per cent of boys and 53 per cent of girls surveyed in 41 countries expect to work in one of just 10 popular jobs by the age of 30 and those expectations are driven by visibility and stereotypes. When girls’ education is tailored to local jobs, you risk tightening that already narrow band of “acceptable” choices even further.

The charity sector has a vital role to play here, and it’s barely mentioned in education reform conversations. UK programmes like our Girls Mean Business campaign, which is calling for young women to be introduced to entrepreneurship and more female founders, are being launched because we know more girls want to launch their own business, but they don’t know where to start. And they can barely name a female entrepreneur. When you give young people access to role models and exposure to careers beyond their immediate geography, amazing things can happen.

open image in gallery Girls around the age of 14 are at their lowest levels of self-confidence – this is when they need to be inspired ( PA )

These grassroots interventions are critical to addressing the challenge Alan Milburn’s recent report on youth employment highlighted: nearly a million young people are not in education, employment or training, and the problem is getting worse.

Milburn’s diagnosis was stark. The Neet crisis is grounded in social disadvantage, with young people from lower working-class backgrounds recording a rate of 22 per cent compared with 9 per cent for those from higher professional backgrounds. Technical skills matter for breaking that cycle, but they are not enough on their own.

We're asking girls to solve global problems with a postcode-sized toolkit

The regional devolution Burnham is championing is genuinely important. Local people making local decisions, understanding their own economies, coordinating schools with employers in their area, that’s brilliant. But we can’t confuse local decision-making with local horizons. These are not the same thing.

We live in a global world. The challenges that the next generation faces – climate change, AI, and the future of work – need global ideas and a diverse set of people to create solutions that work for everyone. If girls are told their education should prepare them only for jobs that exist locally, we're asking them to solve global problems with a postcode-sized toolkit.

Technical skills are essential, but so is aspiration. Andy Burnham's reforms could be genuinely transformative if they work. But only if true parity is achieved and they don't mistake tailoring to local needs with limiting young people's horizons.

Only if they build in the role of charities and role models who can show young people what becomes possible when you dream beyond your postcode. The evidence is clear: visibility shifts aspiration. Without it, we'll simply cement the choices the world has already narrowed for young people by age 14.

Amna Ahmad is the CEO of Inspiring Girls International

News.title: Recovery aids and building muscle: Welsh weightlifter Laura Hughes answers your questions
News.content:
Laura Hughes first discovered weightlifting while training at her local Crossfit gym, making the transition from amateur gym-goer to competitive lifting.

Now a member of the Welsh national weightlifting squad, the 33-year-old holds the Welsh record for both the snatch and the clean and jerk (the two official competitive lifts in weightlifting) and is currently third overall in the women’s Welsh rankings. Hughes won bronze at the 2018 Commonwealth Games in Australia and was selected again for this summer’s Games in Glasgow.

We caught up with her for our Readers Ask series, where industry specialists answer questions from our Telegraph Recommended Reader Panel.

Who inspired you to get into weightlifting?

Olamilekan, South East

Originally, it was lots of different people, particularly general gym goers who were doing weightlifting at my gym. As I’ve grown as an athlete and become more competitive, I’ve had other inspirations.

Most notably, coming into [the Commonwealth Games], it has to be Gareth [Evans], our coach. Looking back at his performance in 2018 when he won his gold medal is so inspiring. [English lifter] Emily Godley was another competitor in 2018. She won the gold medal in my category and I just remember thinking that she was on fire that day.

What are the best exercises for you to build muscle mass?

Norman, Wales

We spend a lot of time doing our main lifts, so snatches, clean and jerks, but we also do lots of pulls and squats. I spend a lot of time doing accessory work to make sure that my body stays healthy, especially being an older athlete. I’ve put on quite a lot of muscle in this last block just from going heavier and pushing my limits with my main lifts.

What advice would you give to people who want to improve their strength?

David, North West

The most important thing is consistency. As long as you’re doing something, do it regularly, even if it’s twice a week. Don’t be afraid of picking up some dumbbells. If you’ve got somebody that can teach you how to lift weights properly, that’s going to be the best option. Do it safely, do it consistently, and don’t be afraid to try new strength exercises.

News.title: Explosive mpox outbreak causes 3,000 cases in Madagascar
News.content:
More than 3,000 cases of mpox have been recorded in Madagascar after the virus spread from a single port city to some of the country’s busiest coastal hubs.

A total of 3,022 cases and 20 deaths have been recorded as of this week, with cases in Toamasina and Taolagnaro accounting for more than half of all diagnoses.

The outbreak has been linked to Clade 1b mpox, a strain that emerged in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 2024, prompting the World Health Organization (WHO) to declare a global public health emergency at the time.

“The main factor driving the continued spread of the disease is human mobility, seeding new outbreaks in areas where the virus has not circulated before,” Professor Carlos Maluquer de Motes of the University of Surrey told The Telegraph.

“Under-reporting is likely, with the real number of cases exceeding what is being reported.”

News.title: Chelsea in 10-goal thriller as ‘Alonso ball’ brings risk and reward
News.content:
Chelsea’s first match under the management of Xabi Alonso was a 10-goal thriller in Australia, as the Premier League side eventually showed their class in a 6-4 win over Western Sydney Wanderers.

Star striker João Pedro, who was controversially left out of Brazil’s World Cup squad, scored a nine-minute hat-trick after coming off the bench with half an hour of the friendly remaining.

Alonso had selected a youthful team for the first hour before bringing nine senior players, including João Pedro, into the side in the second half. According to Transfermarkt, Chelsea’s squad is valued at over £1.3bn while their opponents a more modest £5.86m.

Teenage signing Dastan Satpayev, midfielder Dario Essugo and winger Jamie Gittens also found the net for Chelsea, who were defensively vulnerable for long spells for the game.

Here are five things Telegraph Sport learned from Alonso’s first match.

João Pedro picks up where he left off

João Pedro scored 13 goals in the second half of last season and his impressive performances resulted in the 24-year-old being named Chelsea’s player of the campaign. It was something of a surprise, then, when he was left out of Carlo Ancelotti’s Brazil squad this summer.

The good news for Chelsea is that João Pedro’s absence from the World Cup has given him plenty of time to recover ahead of the new campaign, and he looked thrillingly sharp in his second-half performance against Western Sydney Wanderers. The difference in class between João Pedro and Liam Delap, the man he replaced, was clear for all to see.

Two of the Brazilian’s three goals were classy, composed finishes — and he also created a goal for Gittens after surging past three defenders on the left wing. João Pedro looks like he means business.
