A State Monopoly on Lithium

For foreign investors, Mexico’s lithium landscape changed decisively in 2022 when the government nationalized the mineral, declaring it a strategic resource reserved exclusively for the state.

The decree created Litio para México, known as LitioMX, a decentralized public agency with the sole mandate to explore, extract, and commercialize lithium.

No private concessions for lithium mining are permitted. The legal framework bars foreign and domestic private companies from owning lithium reserves or production.

This model mirrors approaches in other resource-nationalist economies, but it leaves international investors watching from the sidelines unless mixed-investment or service-contract frameworks eventually emerge.

Inside the 2026-2030 Program

The newly published institutional program sets six objectives for LitioMX through the end of the decade.

First, the company aims to consolidate exploration, evaluation, and technical management of Mexico’s lithium resources.

Second, it will promote technology to produce active materials for batteries. Third, it plans to establish a small-scale industrial plant to manufacture battery packs.

Additional goals include developing energy-storage projects, advancing circular-economy and performance-improving technologies, and strengthening the regulatory framework for the lithium sector.

The document does not specify a total investment figure, a production capacity, or a concrete extraction flowsheet for any particular deposit.

The Sonora Deposits and Unrealized Potential

Mexico’s most promising lithium resources lie in the state of Sonora, primarily in clay deposits that are geologically complex and commercially untested at scale.

Unlike South America’s brine-based lithium or Australia’s hard-rock spodumene, Sonora’s clay deposits require processing technology that is still being developed globally.

The institutional program confirms a broader Sonora-focused strategy, but the published sources do not verify a finalized extraction plan for a specific deposit such as Bacadehuachi.

Analysts at Speyside Group have noted that Mexico has yet to unlock its lithium opportunity, citing technological hurdles and the absence of a clear path to commercial production.

Budget Constraints and the Pilot Plant

Despite the ambitious program, LitioMX faces immediate financial limitations. Bloomberg Línea reported that the company will remain without investment spending in the 2026 budget proposal.

El Financiero separately noted that LitioMX would only have budget for payroll in 2026, underscoring the gap between strategic rhetoric and fiscal reality.

The small-scale battery pack plant represents a tangible first step, but without capital expenditure funding, the timeline for construction and operation remains uncertain.

No confirmed project partners have been announced for the battery plant or lithium processing plans in the available official documents.

What Foreign Investors Should Watch

The 2026-2030 program signals the government’s intent to move beyond resource nationalism into downstream battery manufacturing, but execution capability is unproven.

Investors should monitor whether Mexico’s broader mixed-investment infrastructure plan, valued at roughly US$325 billion for 2026-2030, eventually creates openings for private participation in lithium-related projects.

Legal firms such as Jones Day have highlighted recent reforms that unlock private investment in strategic infrastructure, though lithium extraction remains firmly under state control.

For now, the opportunity for foreign capital is limited to potential service contracts, technology licensing, or participation in downstream energy-storage projects that do not involve ownership of the resource itself.

The Sonora deposits remain a long-term proposition. Any progress on extraction technology or pilot processing results will be critical signals for the market.

The Road Ahead

LitioMX’s institutional program provides a policy roadmap, but the absence of a dedicated investment budget for 2026 raises questions about near-term milestones.

The battery pack pilot plant, if funded and built, would mark Mexico’s first state-run step into battery manufacturing, a sector dominated by Asian and Western players.

International observers will also track whether the regulatory framework evolves to permit joint ventures or technology partnerships without violating the constitutional ban on private lithium concessions.

For expats and investors following Latin America, Mexico’s lithium story is still in its early chapters, with Sonora’s clay deposits representing both a strategic asset and a technical challenge that has yet to be solved.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is LitioMX and what does it do?

LitioMX (Litio para México) is a decentralized public agency created by the Mexican government in 2022. It holds the exclusive mandate to explore, extract, and commercialize lithium, which was nationalized as a strategic resource.

Can foreign companies invest in Mexico’s lithium sector?

Foreign companies cannot hold lithium mining concessions in Mexico. The constitutional framework reserves lithium exclusively for the state.

Potential opportunities may exist through service contracts, technology licensing, or downstream projects that do not involve resource ownership.

Where are Mexico’s main lithium deposits located?

Mexico’s most significant lithium resources are in the state of Sonora, primarily in clay deposits. These deposits are geologically complex and require processing technology that is not yet commercially proven at scale.

World.title: Bolivia Investment: Paz Secures US$300 Million
World.content:
Bolivia · Business

Key Facts —Bolivia Investment President Rodrigo Paz announced about US$300 million for a highway, Amazon power and police, funded by CAF and the IDB. —Highway project Funds target the Santa Bárbara-Caranavi highway in the Los Yungas area of La Paz department, a key transport link in a rugged agricultural region. —Amazon electricity A portion of the financing supports electrical integration in Bolivia’s Amazon region, building on a prior US$204 million IDB loan for the same purpose. —Police modernization The package includes resources to modernize the Bolivian Police, though specific equipment or training details have not been released. —Broader context The announcement marks the Paz government’s first major investment push backed by multilateral lenders since taking office, amid a severe foreign-exchange shortage.

President Rodrigo Paz announced a roughly US$300 million Bolivia La Paz investment package on July 26, 2026, targeting a key highway, Amazon-region electrical integration, and police modernization. The financing, the new government’s first major push backed by multilateral lenders, comes from the CAF (Development Bank of Latin America and the Caribbean) and the IDB (Inter-American Development Bank).

What the US$300 Million Package Funds

The roughly US$300 million package covers three distinct areas. The first is the Santa Bárbara-Caranavi highway, located in the Los Yungas region of La Paz department, a mountainous, agriculturally important zone northeast of the capital city.

A Separate La Paz City Package

During a civic anniversary session for La Paz’s 217th year, President Paz also outlined a local investment package of roughly Bs 1 billion. This city-focused spending targets road infrastructure, including the Escoma-Charazani highway, completion of the Unduavi-Chulumani route, and bridges at four river crossings.

Economic Context for Foreign Readers

The roughly US$300 million multilateral package is the Paz government’s first big investment push since taking office. Bolivia faces a severe foreign-exchange shortage, dwindling gas exports, and inflation pressures that prompted an IMF agreement earlier in 2026.

Political Significance of the Announcement

Paz chose the sesión de honor for La Paz’s 217th civic anniversary to unveil the roughly US$300 million package. The timing underscores the political importance of the department, a traditional stronghold of opposition to the former ruling Movement Toward Socialism party.

What Comes Next for Investors

Foreign investors should watch for the finalized terms of the CAF and IDB financing agreements. The exact disbursement schedules, procurement rules, and project timelines will determine near-term opportunities.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much is the Bolivia La Paz investment package worth?

President Rodrigo Paz announced roughly US$300 million in financing from CAF and the IDB for a highway in La Paz department’s Los Yungas region, electrical integration in the Amazon, and police modernization.

What does the Santa Bárbara-Caranavi highway project involve?

The project funds rehabilitation of the Santa Bárbara-Caranavi road in the Los Yungas area of La Paz department. It is one of three components in the roughly US$300 million multilateral financing package.

Is the La Paz city package the same as the US$300 million announcement?

No. The roughly US$300 million package is funded by multilateral lenders for a highway, Amazon electricity, and police modernization. A separate La Paz city package, announced in bolivianos, totals about Bs 1 billion for local roads, health, water, and other municipal projects.

World.title: Dominican Republic Electricity Demand Hits 4,203 MW Record
World.content:
Caribbean · Business

Key Facts —Dominican Republic Electricity Demand National electricity demand hit a record 4,203 MW on July 27, 2026, per the Energy Ministry. —Previous record 4,195.26 MW set on Wednesday, July 24, 2026, just four days earlier. —July records The July 28 peak was the fourth all-time demand record set during the month. —System stability The SENI grid met the record load without blackouts, maintaining stable nationwide supply. —Primary drivers Intense summer heat and increased consumption from economic growth.

Dominican Republic electricity demand surged to an unprecedented 4,203 megawatts (MW) on Monday, July 28, 2026, setting a new all-time high for the Caribbean nation’s power grid as a relentless summer heat wave and accelerating economic activity pushed the system to its latest peak.

Electricity transmission lines (illustrative). Photo: Wikimedia Commons.

A Month of Broken Records

The milestone was recorded at exactly 8:56 p.m. local time within the Sistema Eléctrico Nacional Interconectado (SENI), the national interconnected grid that serves the majority of the country’s 11 million residents. The grid’s coordinating body, known as the Organismo Coordinador (OC-SENI), confirmed the figure.

This new peak shattered the previous record of 4,195.26 MW, which had been set just four days earlier on Wednesday, July 24, 2026, at 9:32 p.m. That benchmark itself had eclipsed a record of 4,185.11 MW established only a day before, on Tuesday, July 23.

The sequence of broken records began earlier in the month, with demand reaching 4,166.52 MW on Thursday, July 16, 2026, at 9:58 p.m. The July 28 peak therefore represents the fourth time the country’s electricity consumption hit an all-time high in under two weeks.

The Heat Factor: Cooling a Tropical Economy

For foreign residents and investors accustomed to the Dominican Republic’s year-round warmth, the summer of 2026 has been exceptional. A prolonged heat wave has blanketed the region, driving residents and businesses to rely heavily on air conditioning, particularly during the evening peak hours when families return home.

Unlike temperate-zone grids that peak in winter for heating, tropical electricity systems like the SENI are summer-peaking. The record-setting times – consistently between 8:56 p.m. and 9:58 p.m. – highlight how residential cooling demand after sunset, combined with still-warm temperatures, creates the maximum strain on generation and transmission infrastructure.

The Ministry of Energy and Mines attributed the surge directly to high temperatures and increased consumption. This pattern mirrors trends seen across other warm-climate grids globally, where more frequent and intense heat waves are shifting baseline demand expectations upward.

Economic Growth Adds to Grid Strain

Beyond the weather, structural economic expansion is a major driver of the Dominican Republic’s rising electricity appetite. The country has been one of Latin America’s top-performing economies, with growth fueled by tourism, free-trade zones, construction, and foreign direct investment.

More economic activity means more commercial office towers, manufacturing lines, hotels, and logistics centers drawing power throughout the day. This rising base load means that when a heat wave spikes residential cooling demand, the starting point is already higher than in previous years.

For expat entrepreneurs and real estate investors, the growing demand signals a market with expanding energy needs. It also underscores the importance of the government’s ongoing efforts to modernize generation capacity and diversify the energy matrix to keep pace with consumption.

Grid Stability Amid the Stress Test

Despite the record strain, the SENI system held firm. Official reports explicitly stated that the grid was able to cover the increase in consumption while maintaining stable service nationwide, with no blackouts reported during the peak event.

This outcome represents a significant achievement for a country that has historically struggled with power reliability. For decades, blackouts and voltage fluctuations were a frustrating reality for households and a cost of doing business for companies operating on the island.

The stable performance under maximum stress suggests that recent investments in generation plants and transmission infrastructure are delivering results. For foreign investors, grid reliability is a critical factor when evaluating the Dominican Republic as a destination for operations that require uninterrupted power, such as data centers or advanced manufacturing.

What This Means for Foreigners and Investors

For the expat community and international businesses, the record demand carries both reassurance and a cautionary note. The grid’s ability to meet 4,203 MW without incident is a positive signal of improved resilience in the country’s electricity sector.

However, a series of broken records in rapid succession indicates that the margin between peak demand and available generation may be narrowing. While the exact installed capacity of the SENI was not specified in the July 28 report, sustained demand growth will require continued capacity expansion to maintain the stability demonstrated during this event.

Investors in tourism, real estate, and industry should monitor future announcements from the Ministry of Energy and Mines regarding generation projects. The Dominican Republic has been actively incorporating natural gas and renewable energy sources, a diversification strategy that becomes more urgent as consumption records fall with increasing frequency.

The Broader Regional Context

The Dominican Republic’s demand spike is not occurring in isolation. Across the hemisphere, grids from the United States to Brazil have been setting summer records as heat waves become more intense and persistent.

The largest US grid, PJM Interconnection, also reported record demand in early July 2026.

For Latin America, where air conditioning penetration is still growing, the upward trajectory of electricity demand is expected to be steeper than in more mature markets. The Dominican Republic, with its high tourism exposure and expanding middle class, sits at the intersection of these trends.

As the country continues to position itself as a hub for nearshoring and digital nomads, a reliable and scalable electricity system will be fundamental. The events of July 2026 offer a real-world test that, for now, the grid has passed.

Frequently Asked Questions

What was the new record for Dominican Republic electricity demand?

The national electricity demand reached a new all-time high of 4,203 MW on Monday, July 28, 2026, at 8:56 p.m., according to the Ministry of Energy and Mines and the grid operator OC-SENI.

Why is electricity demand spiking in the Dominican Republic?

The surge is driven primarily by an intense summer heat wave that has increased air conditioning use, combined with rising base consumption from sustained economic growth in tourism, construction, and free-trade zones.

Did the record electricity demand cause blackouts?

No. Official reports confirmed that the SENI grid was able to meet the 4,203 MW peak load while maintaining stable service nationwide, with no blackouts reported during the event.

World.title: Portonave Plans US$392M Navegantes Port Expansion
World.content:
Brazil · Business

Key Facts —Portonave Navegantes Portonave will invest R$2 billion (~US$392 million) to expand the Navegantes container terminal in Santa Catarina. —Capacity target Annual container handling capacity to rise from 1.5 million TEU to 2 million TEU after completion. —Depth target Access channel and berthing depth to move from under 14 meters to 17 meters, dependent on a separate federal concession. —Timeline Works began in January 2024, with the first stage completed in September 2025 and the second stage running through the second half of 2026. —Ownership The terminal is controlled by Terminal Investment Limited (TiL), the ports arm of Swiss-based shipping giant Mediterranean Shipping Company (MSC).

Portonave Navegantes, the Santa Catarina container terminal controlled by MSC’s Terminal Investment Limited (TiL), is pushing forward with a roughly R$2 billion (~US$392 million) modernization plan. The private terminal aims to lift its annual capacity from 1.5 million to 2 million TEU and prepare for a deeper access channel, intensifying a capacity race among southern Brazil’s ports.

A Brazilian container port (illustrative). Photo: Wikimedia Commons.

The Modernization Blueprint

Portonave’s investment is not an area expansion but a densification and upgrade of its existing footprint in Navegantes, on the northern coast of Santa Catarina state. The company detailed a spending split of R$1.6 billion (~US$314 million) for quay reinforcement and civil works, plus R$439 million (~US$86 million) for new, fully electric equipment.

The terminal’s current annual capacity of 1.5 million TEU – a standard measure for a twenty-foot container – will climb to 2 million TEU. This boost is designed to handle larger vessels and higher cargo volumes without physically expanding the terminal’s perimeter.

A critical enabler is the planned deepening of the access channel and berthing area from less than 14 meters currently to a target of 17 meters. This dredging, however, is not part of Portonave’s private investment but hinges on a separate public concession for the port channel, which was under review by Brazil’s federal audit court, the TCU.

The Southern Brazil Port Race

For foreign investors, Portonave’s move is a direct response to a structural shift in global shipping. Container lines are deploying ever-larger vessels, often exceeding 366 meters in length, which require deeper drafts and longer quays.

Ports that cannot accommodate these ships risk being relegated to feeder status, losing direct calls to regional hubs.

Southern Brazil is witnessing a concentrated capacity race. Portonave, already one of the country’s top container terminals by volume, competes directly with nearby terminals like Port of Itapoá and Portonave’s own neighbor, the public Port of Itajaí, just across the river.

Further south, in Santos, Latin America’s largest port, a separate multibillion-dollar auction for a new container terminal is advancing.

Consultancy reports cited in Brazilian media project that Brazilian ports collectively foresee over R$10 billion in works to increase capacity and receive larger ships. The logic is simple: a port that can handle a 400-meter vessel on a direct Asia-South America route captures cargo that would otherwise be transshipped, reducing logistics costs for exporters and importers.

Portonave’s private nature gives it an agility advantage. As a private-use terminal, it can fast-track investments without the lengthy public bidding processes that constrain federally administered ports.

This model has attracted global terminal operators like TiL/MSC, which view Brazilian agribusiness and industrial exports as a long-term growth corridor.

MSC’s Strategic Footprint

Terminal Investment Limited, the ports arm of Mediterranean Shipping Company, controls Portonave. MSC is the world’s largest container line by capacity.

For an investor, TiL’s deepening commitment signals a strategic bet on Santa Catarina as a core node in MSC’s South American network.

Owning a terminal allows a carrier to guarantee berthing windows, control costs, and optimize its service loops. Portonave’s expansion aligns with MSC’s global pattern of securing dedicated infrastructure in key export markets.

The terminal’s modernization directly supports the carrier’s ability to deploy its largest neo-Panamax vessels on Brazilian routes.

Timeline and Execution

The modernization is being executed in stages. The first stage began in January 2024 and was completed in September 2025.

The second stage is underway and scheduled for completion by the end of 2026, or the second half of 2026, according to company statements.

Portonave has publicly expressed urgency regarding the federal channel concession. The terminal’s full potential to receive the deepest-draft vessels remains locked until the access channel is dredged to 17 meters.

Without this public-sector piece, the private quay upgrades alone cannot deliver the full navigational capability.

What This Means for Foreign Investors

The expansion underscores a broader investment thesis for Brazilian infrastructure. The country’s port sector has attracted significant foreign capital since regulatory reforms allowed private terminals to handle third-party cargo.

Portonave’s R$2 billion plan is a tangible example of a global terminal operator doubling down on this framework.

For expat entrepreneurs and foreign funds, the capacity race signals both opportunity and risk. Improved port infrastructure lowers export logistics costs for Brazilian commodities and manufactured goods, potentially boosting margins for producers. Conversely, terminals that fail to keep pace with the depth and scale requirements may see volumes migrate to better-equipped rivals.

The Santa Catarina port complex, including Navegantes, Itapoá, and Itajaí, is a critical gateway for Brazil’s southern and midwestern export corridors, particularly for frozen proteins, wood products, and machinery. Portonave’s investment helps secure the region’s relevance in global trade lanes for the next decade.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who owns Portonave Navegantes?

Portonave is controlled by Terminal Investment Limited (TiL), the ports division of Mediterranean Shipping Company (MSC), the world’s largest container shipping line.

How much is Portonave investing and what will it achieve?

Portonave is investing roughly R$2 billion (~US$392 million) to modernize its quay and buy new equipment. The project will lift annual container capacity from 1.5 million to 2 million TEU and prepare the terminal for a deeper 17-meter access channel.

When will the Portonave expansion be completed?

The first stage was completed in September 2025. The second stage is ongoing and is scheduled for completion by the second half of 2026.

The deeper access channel depends on a separate federal concession process.

World.title: Jamaica GCT Hike Threatens Caribbean Holiday Costs
World.content:
Caribbean · Business

Key Facts —Jamaica GCT Hike The tourism GCT is set to rise from 10% to 15% by April 2027, phased over two fiscal years. —Implementation date The increase is deferred until 1 April 2027, giving the industry a transition period. —Government revenue target The measure is projected to generate approximately J$11.4 billion (~US$73.6 million) in additional annual revenue. —Industry position The Jamaica Hotel and Tourist Association (JHTA) has rejected the proposal, calling a 50% tax increase untenable during ongoing recovery. —Current tourism tax Jamaica currently applies a reduced 10% GCT rate to specified tourism activities, compared to the standard 15% applied to most other goods and services.

Jamaica GCT on tourism activities is set to rise from 10% to 15% under a government proposal deferred to April 2027, a move that has triggered fierce opposition from hotel operators who argue it will drive up holiday costs for international visitors and weaken the island’s competitive edge in the Caribbean.

A resort in Negril, Jamaica. Photo: Wikimedia Commons.

What the Tax Change Means for Travelers

For foreign visitors booking a Jamaican holiday, the proposed increase in the General Consumption Tax (GCT) would directly raise the final bill. The GCT is a value-added tax applied to specified tourism activities, including hotel accommodation, tours, and certain dining services.

A five-percentage-point rise may sound modest, but industry leaders emphasize the practical impact. Moving from 10% to 15% represents a 50% increase in the tax burden on affected services, according to the Jamaica Hotel and Tourist Association (JHTA).

A traveler paying US$300 per night for a hotel room currently pays roughly US$30 in GCT. Under the new rate, that same room would attract US$45 in tax, adding US$15 nightly.

Over a week-long stay, the extra cost reaches US$105 before factoring in tours or other taxed activities.

This incremental cost could shift traveler behavior. Budget-conscious tourists from the United States, Canada, and Europe may begin comparing total package prices more closely with rival destinations like the Dominican Republic, Mexico’s Riviera Maya, or The Bahamas, where tax structures on tourism differ.

Government Rationale: Ending ‘Differential Treatment’

The Jamaican government has framed the increase as a necessary step to meet medium-term revenue needs. The Ministry of Finance argues the tourism sector has matured enough to absorb the higher rate after years of benefiting from what it calls ‘prolonged differential treatment.’

The standard GCT rate across Jamaica is 15%. Tourism has enjoyed a reduced 10% rate, a concession the government now views as unsustainable given fiscal pressures.

The measure is estimated to yield about J$11.4 billion (~US$73.6 million) in additional annual revenue.

The proposal emerged from the 2026/2027 budget cycle, with revenue measures detailed in summaries published by major accounting firms EY, KPMG, and PwC in February 2026. The government projects J$29.4 billion (~US$190 million) from new revenue measures in fiscal year 2026/27, with the tourism GCT adjustment forming a significant component.

Prime Minister Andrew Holness has described the decision to introduce new taxes as a last resort, according to regional media reports. The deferral to April 2027 was designed to give operators time to adjust pricing and contracts.

Industry Pushback: ‘A 50% Tax Increase’

The JHTA has flatly rejected the proposal. In statements reported by the Jamaica Observer and Our Today, the association argues the increase is untenable for a sector still navigating post-pandemic recovery challenges, rising operational costs, and intense regional competition.

Industry representatives dispute the government’s framing of a five-point adjustment. They stress that moving from 10% to 15% constitutes a 50% GCT increase, not a marginal change.

The Jamaica Observer quoted industry voices warning the hike could make Jamaica a ‘sitting duck’ for competitors.

The JHTA has sought direct talks with Prime Minister Holness to discuss the proposed increase, signaling the seriousness of the rift. Hoteliers argue that even with a deferral to 2027, the tax creates uncertainty for forward bookings, which in the Caribbean often occur 12 to 18 months in advance.

Operators also point to the compounding effect of other costs. Jamaica’s tourism sector already faces high electricity expenses, insurance premiums, and labor costs. Adding a higher consumption tax, they contend, will squeeze margins or force price increases that reduce demand.

Competitiveness in the Caribbean Market

Jamaica competes directly with other Caribbean nations for North American and European tourists. Tax policy forms part of the total cost equation alongside airlift availability, room rates, and perceived value.

Several competing destinations apply different tax models. Some levy room taxes or departure taxes rather than broad consumption taxes on tourism services.

A higher GCT in Jamaica could make all-inclusive packages appear more expensive in online travel agency comparisons, where price sorting is a dominant user behavior.

For foreign investors in Jamaican hospitality assets, the tax increase introduces a new variable into revenue projections. Higher end-consumer costs could pressure occupancy rates if travelers shift to lower-tax jurisdictions.

Alternatively, hotels may absorb part of the tax to maintain competitiveness, compressing profit margins.

The deferral to April 2027 provides a window for investors to model scenarios. However, the uncertainty surrounding the final rate – should industry lobbying succeed in reducing or scrapping the hike – complicates long-term planning for resort developments and renovations currently in the pipeline.

What Happens Next

The proposal is tied to the 2026/2027 budget cycle, meaning legislative action would formalize the increase. The government has not signaled a willingness to retreat, but the JHTA’s direct engagement with the Prime Minister’s office indicates negotiations are active.

Travelers with existing bookings for dates after April 2027 should monitor the situation. Contracts typically allow for tax changes to be passed through, though operators may choose to honor pre-increase pricing to preserve goodwill.

For the broader Caribbean tourism landscape, Jamaica’s decision could set a precedent. If the island successfully implements the 15% rate without significant demand erosion, other cash-strapped governments in the region may revisit their own tourism tax structures.

The Jamaica Observer’s July 2026 coverage captured the industry’s mood as defiant, with operators vowing to fight the measure. The coming months will reveal whether fiscal imperatives or industry competitiveness arguments prevail.

Practical Advice for Foreign Visitors and Investors

Travelers planning Jamaican holidays should budget for the potential increase. A family spending US$5,000 on accommodation and taxed services could face roughly US$250 in additional GCT costs if the 15% rate takes effect.

Investors should closely track the JHTA-government dialogue. Any compromise – such as a phased implementation or exemptions for certain tourism sub-sectors – would materially affect asset valuations and return forecasts.

Monitoring official sources is advisable. The Jamaica Information Service (JIS) publishes government announcements, while the JHTA and major accounting firms provide updates on regulatory changes.

The April 2027 implementation date remains the key milestone, but political dynamics could shift the timeline or outcome.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the current GCT rate on tourism in Jamaica?

Currently, specified tourism activities in Jamaica are subject to a reduced General Consumption Tax (GCT) rate of 10%, compared to the standard 15% rate applied to most other goods and services.

When will the Jamaica GCT increase take effect?

The proposed increase from 10% to 15% is deferred until 1 April 2027, according to government announcements tied to the 2026/2027 budget cycle.

How much extra will a Jamaica holiday cost under the new GCT?

A traveler paying US$300 per night for accommodation would pay roughly US$45 in GCT instead of US$30, adding US$15 per night. Over a week-long stay, the additional tax burden would be approximately US$105 before other taxed services.

World.title: JBS, Marfrig Cattle Supply Boost as US Reopens Mexico Border
World.content:
Brazil · Business

JBS Marfrig cattle supply prospects improved sharply after the United States government announced a phased reopening of its southern border to Mexican cattle imports, ending a closure triggered by a New World screwworm outbreak. Shares of the Brazilian meatpacking giants, which operate massive beef processing networks on US soil, climbed on the news – JBS about 10% and Marfrig’s successor MBRF about 5.5% – as investors bet on easing cattle shortages that have squeezed margins across the American beef industry.

Key Facts —USDA announcement. The USDA announced a phased reopening of southern cattle ports starting August 24, 2026, with Douglas, Arizona. —Screwworm inspections. All cattle entering through reopened ports will receive a full USDA inspection for New World screwworm. —Market reaction. Shares of JBS (JBSS3) rose about 10% and MBRF (MBRF3) – which controls US processor National Beef – gained roughly 5.5%; US peer Tyson climbed about 7%. —Supply chain logic. Reopening Mexican cattle imports eases US cattle shortages, improving availability and potentially lowering input costs for processors. —Phased approach. The reopening is gradual and contingent on Mexico’s progress, with no firm dates yet for ports in New Mexico. RT Ask Rio Times Latin American markets, currencies and companies. The Border Reopening: A Phased Plan

The US Department of Agriculture (USDA) confirmed on July 24, 2026, that it will begin lifting the suspension on Mexican cattle imports. The first port of entry to resume operations will be Douglas, Arizona, set to reopen on August 24.

The federal announcement specified that the Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) would then initiate steps to reopen ports in Santa Teresa and Columbus, New Mexico. However, the USDA did not provide firm dates for those subsequent locations, stressing that the entire process is contingent on Mexico’s adherence to a joint action plan.

To mitigate risk, every single animal entering through the reopened ports will undergo a full USDA inspection for New World screwworm. Officials noted that as of July 22, the nearest active screwworm case was approximately 325 miles away from the Douglas entry point.

The phased design means the supply relief will be gradual. The USDA explicitly warned that the reopening could be paused or adjusted if the epidemiological risk changes, adding a layer of uncertainty for cattle buyers.

Why Mexican Cattle Matter to US Beef Processors

The United States cattle herd has been contracting, making the country increasingly reliant on imported feeder cattle from Mexico to sustain its beef production capacity. Mexico is a critical supplier of lightweight cattle that are sent to American feedlots to be fattened before slaughter.

When the border closed due to the screwworm detection, that vital artery of livestock was severed. US beef processors, particularly those operating in border states, faced a tightening supply of animals just as domestic cattle prices remained elevated.

This dynamic creates a classic margin squeeze: processors must pay high prices for scarce cattle while competing in wholesale beef markets where prices cannot always keep pace. Reopening imports directly addresses the supply side of that equation, potentially lowering procurement costs for slaughterhouses.

For companies with large US slaughter and processing footprints, even a partial restoration of Mexican cattle flows can materially improve plant utilization rates and operating margins. The market reaction reflects this direct link between border policy and processor profitability.

The company is involved in the production and marketing of prepared foods and other related products, as well as operations in leather, collagen, hygiene and beauty products, metal packaging,…

The Brazilian Giants’ American Footprint

To understand why a US border policy moves stocks on Brazil’s B3 exchange, foreign investors must grasp the scale of JBS and Marfrig in the United States. JBS USA is one of the largest beef processors in the country, operating numerous slaughterhouses and fabricating facilities.

Marfrig – now part of the merged group MBRF – controls its US exposure through National Beef Packing Company, the fourth-largest US beef processor. For both Brazilian parent companies, the North American market represents a dominant share of total revenue and operational profit.

When US cattle supply tightens, the earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) generated by these American subsidiaries comes under direct pressure. Conversely, any policy that loosens cattle supply is a tailwind for their largest profit centers.

The share moves after the announcement – JBS up about 10% and MBRF (MBRF3) about 5.5% – reflect the market’s rapid recalculation of the earnings power of these US-domiciled assets. At an exchange rate of 5.1 Brazilian reais to the US dollar (USD/BRL 5.1), every dollar of improved margin in the US translates into a significant boost to consolidated results reported in reais.

The New World Screwworm Threat

The New World screwworm (Cochliomyia hominivorax) is a parasitic fly whose larvae feed on the living tissue of warm-blooded animals, including cattle. An infestation can be fatal if untreated, making it a devastating threat to livestock herds.

The screwworm was officially eradicated from the United States in 1966 and from Mexico by 1991, following a decades-long sterile insect technique program. However, it persists in parts of South America and the Caribbean, creating a constant risk of reintroduction through the movement of infested animals.

The detection of new cases in Mexico prompted the USDA to suspend cattle imports as a biosecurity measure to protect the US herd. The phased reopening signals that authorities believe the immediate outbreak is being contained, but the rigorous inspection protocol at ports like Douglas underscores that the threat is not considered eliminated.

For foreign investors unfamiliar with agricultural biosecurity, this episode illustrates how a single veterinary health issue can disrupt a multi-billion-dollar cross-border supply chain. The market’s sensitivity to the reopening highlights just how fragile the just-in-time livestock supply system can be.

Market Implications and Gradual Recovery

While the share price reaction was immediate, the actual flow of cattle into the United States will be a slow trickle before it becomes a stream. With only the Douglas, Arizona port opening on August 24, and no timeline for the larger New Mexico crossings, the total volume of imported cattle will initially be limited.

Analysts caution that the full benefit to processor margins will take quarters to materialize. The cattle feeding cycle means that animals imported as feeders in late August will not reach slaughter weight for several months, delaying the impact on beef production volumes.

Furthermore, the USDA’s cautious tone and the conditionality of the reopening introduce political and sanitary risk. Any new screwworm detection near the border could halt imports again, creating volatility for companies like JBS and MBRF that have become structurally dependent on binational cattle flows.

For long-term investors in Brazilian protein exporters, the episode reinforces a key thesis: these are effectively global companies whose operational fortunes are dictated by sanitary policies and cattle cycles in their host countries, not just demand in their home market.

Frequently Asked Questions Why did JBS and Marfrig shares jump on the US border reopening? JBS and Marfrig own massive beef processing operations in the United States. The reopening of the border to Mexican cattle eases a supply shortage, which is expected to lower input costs and improve profit margins for their US plants. What is the New World screwworm and why did it close the border? The New World screwworm is a parasitic fly whose larvae eat the living flesh of animals. The US closed its border to Mexican cattle to prevent the parasite from spreading to the American herd, as an infestation can be fatal to livestock. When will Mexican cattle actually start entering the US again? The first port of entry, Douglas, Arizona, is scheduled to reopen on August 24, 2026. Reopenings for ports in Santa Teresa and Columbus, New Mexico, will follow, but no firm dates have been announced for those locations.

World.title: Why “Diablo” Got Only Three Months in Costa Rica Custody
World.content:
A Costa Rican court has ordered three months and 22 days of preventive detention for a man surnamed Arias, known by the alias “Diablo,” in a resolution issued yesterday. The term runs from the date of his detention on July 24 to November 16, 2026. In the same resolution, the court imposed five months and 26 days on a co-defendant surnamed Pérez, alias “Tan,” a period that expires on December 27, 2026.

The numbers were read by much of us as an anticlimax, and the criticism reached the top of the executive branch. Before the Public Ministry issued its explanation, President Laura Fernández said publicly that a three-month term would be the greatest embarrassment the judiciary could produce. Legislator Kattia Calvo separately questioned the result. Neither reaction accounted for what the Public Ministry set out hours later, which is that the terms are a statutory ceiling rather than a measure of how seriously the court treats the case.

Under ordinary criminal jurisdiction in Costa Rica, preventive detention in a single case is capped at 18 months. Both men had already spent time in preventive custody during earlier stages of this same file. What the Tribunal Penal del II Circuito Judicial de Limón granted yesterday was not a fresh term but the unused remainder of that 18-month allowance — three months and 22 days left for Arias, five months and 26 days for Pérez.

The Fiscalía Adjunta contra la Delincuencia Organizada asked for exactly those figures because they were the only ones available to it. The hearing began at 1:30 p.m. and was held in private at the Tribunales del I Circuito Judicial de San José, moved there from Pococí for security reasons.

November 16 is therefore a procedural checkpoint rather than a release date. The Public Ministry has said the expiry of the term does not mean either man automatically walks free, and that it will seek an extension before the Tribunal Penal de Apelación de Sentencia, the body that decides preventive detention once the ordinary 18-month limit has been exhausted.

The court also declared the case one of organized crime, applying article 10, subsection 1 of Law 9481, which created Costa Rica’s specialized organized crime jurisdiction. That declaration moves the file out of ordinary jurisdiction, and the Public Ministry has said it will ask the specialized tribunal to take over several of the causes against both men. If that request is granted, the maximum preventive detention terms available in the case can double.

The file on which yesterday’s order was issued concerns two homicides and one attempted homicide, allegedly committed as contract killings, along with a charge of criminal association. The events under investigation date to Pococí in 2015. Neither man has been tried, and both remain presumed innocent.

If you don’t know by now, both were detained during an operation in Sarapiquí that the Organismo de Investigación Judicial named Operation Némesis. Agents were met with gunfire on entering the property, and the exchange lasted roughly an hour. Five OIJ officers were wounded, one seriously enough to be flown to San José by helicopter.

A third man, surnamed Ríos Oconitrillo and known as “Coco Guácimo,” was killed by after firing on agents. Investigators later reported recovering assault rifles, ammunition and drones from the scene, and estimated that some 2,500 rounds were fired. Arias and Pérez are being held in maximum-security cells at La Reforma.

The scale of the case is what has kept it at the center of national attention. OIJ interim director Michael Soto told a press conference at the Supreme Court that the three criminal structures linked to Arias, Pérez and Ríos Oconitrillo are connected to approximately 360 homicides — around 200 attributed to the first group, 100 to the second and 60 to the third.

Soto was explicit that the figure attaches to the structures rather than to the three men individually, and described it as conservative. He said the organizations controlled drug distribution, cigarette and liquor smuggling and score-settling across Pococí, Sarapiquí, the Northern Zone, Cañas, Liberia, Santa Cruz, Turrialba, Quepos, Parrita, Garabito, Osa, Guácimo, Batán, Valle La Estrella and Nicoya.

Soto also warned that removing the leadership of three structures at once could produce violence rather than calm, as sellers inside and outside those groups move to take territory. The precedent he pointed to is the 2012 capture of a man surnamed Zamora Solórzano, alias “El Indio,” which set off a fight over drug-selling zones in southern San José that left more than 110 people dead by 2015. Zamora was sentenced to 70 years in prison in 2015.

Arias’s defense attorney, Cristian Rodríguez, told reporters that his client’s release had been effectively impossible given the years spent as a fugitive, the gravity of the alleged offenses and the new accusations arising from the July 24 operation. Rodríguez has filed a challenge before the tribunal against security measures imposed on his client by the Ministry of Justice, and has said he may take the matter to the Constitutional Chamber.

What happens on November 16 now depends on two decisions that have not yet been made — whether the appeals tribunal grants the extension the Public Ministry has said it will request, and whether the specialized organized crime tribunal assumes the file. Until then, the date on the resolution marks the limit of what one court was permitted to order, not the length of time anyone expects these men to spend in custody.

World.title: Costa Rica Reworks $400 Million Limón Hospital Tender After Failed Bid
World.content:
Costa Rica’s public health system is preparing to relaunch the tender for a new hospital in Limón during the final week of July, seven months after the first competition for the roughly $400 million project closed without a single company submitting an offer.

The Caja Costarricense de Seguro Social (CCSS) has rewritten the terms of the competition to address the objection contractors raised most consistently the first time around. Under the original terms, the winning firm would have been locked into its quoted price for the full life of a project expected to run several years, with no mechanism to recover cost increases if the exchange rate moved, if steel and cement rose, or if freight became more expensive. Jorge Granados, the CCSS manager of infrastructure and technology, confirmed that the institution has secured a change to that provision for the new tender.

The absence of a price-adjustment clause was not an oversight. The first competition was structured as a turnkey contract covering design, construction and equipment in a single award, and the regulations accompanying the General Public Contracting Law bar price readjustment mechanisms in contracts of that type. Granados told the CCSS board earlier this year that when the institution surveyed the companies that had declined to bid, the inability to adjust prices was the reason they named most often. On a project of this size and duration, he said, ordinary movement in input costs becomes a risk the bidder alone would have to absorb.

Construction firms cited additional concerns. Security conditions in the province and the repeated closures of Route 32, the highway that connects the Caribbean coast to the Central Valley, both came up in the CCSS survey, along with uncertainty over the colón’s behavior against the dollar. The institution has characterized those as secondary to the pricing question, though they help explain why a project in Limón in particular drew no takers.

The second change to the tender is structural. The first competition was open only to companies that had cleared an earlier international prequalification round, which in practice narrowed the field to five Costa Rican firms. Representatives of all five visited the 19-hectare (47-acre) site in June of last year, and none of them bid when the window closed in December. The new process discards prequalification entirely and will be run as an open public tender, which allows companies beyond that original group, including foreign firms, to compete alongside them. Mónica Taylor, the CCSS executive president, has said the institution intends to draw bidders from abroad.

The financial figures attached to the project have shifted with the currency. The tender declared unsuccessful was valued at approximately ¢208.78 billion, a figure set when the colón stood considerably weaker against the dollar than it does now. The CCSS currently describes the project as costing close to $400 million, which at the Banco Central de Costa Rica reference rate of ¢455.40 to the dollar would translate to roughly ¢182 billion. The gap between those two numbers over a period of months is a fair illustration of the exposure contractors said they were unwilling to carry.

How quickly the relaunch translates into visible work on the ground is the open question. Taylor has previously indicated that awarding a contract of this scale would take about a year. Granados has since offered a longer estimate, warning that even with the tender published in the coming days, the contracting and award process for a project of this magnitude can run up to two years before construction begins. Once building starts, he has estimated roughly two and a half years to completion, with late 2029 as a tentative date for the hospital to open its doors.

That timeline sits well beyond what the institution promised the province. In a 2023 press statement the CCSS said the facility would be ready by the end of 2027. President Laura Fernández has asked whether groundbreaking could be scheduled for August 31, 2027, the Day of the Black Person and Afro-Costa Rican Culture, a date that would now mark the start of construction rather than the opening the province was originally told to expect.

The failed tender has drawn official scrutiny. The Defensoría de los Habitantes opened an investigation into the process, requesting that the CCSS submit an improvement plan for the project along with the specific adjustments planned to the tender terms, the contracting model and the participation conditions, and the corrective measures it intends to take in the short, medium and long term. The ombudsman’s office framed the review as a matter of verifying efficiency, reasonableness and transparency in a project it described as essential to the right to health for the population of Limón.

The current Hospital Tony Facio Castro serves the entire Caribbean province, including the cruise port at Limón, the beach communities of Cahuita and Puerto Viejo, and the agricultural districts along Route 32. Its physical condition has been the central argument for replacement for years, and every month the new tender does not produce a contract is another month the province waits on a building the CCSS itself has called urgent.

Whether the revised terms are enough to attract offers will be visible within weeks of publication. If the second competition also closes without bids, the institution will be back at a starting point it has now reached twice.

World.title: Halo BPO hiring work from home sales agents at $8.50 an hour
World.content:
Halo BPO hiring work from home sales agents at $8.50 an hour

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The work from home opportunities keep coming for Belizeans. Halo BPO is recruiting sales agents to work remotely from anywhere in Belize, with pay posted upfront at $8.50 BZD per hour and a dialing schedule of 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. Belize time.

The company says it is looking for qualified candidates only, specifically agents with appointment setting or home improvement sales experience.

The technical requirements are strict, and applicants should check them before applying. Candidates need internet with at least 40 Mbps download and 40 Mbps upload speed on a wired ethernet connection, as Wi-Fi is not allowed. The computer must have a quad core CPU of 2.0GHz or faster and at least 8GB of RAM, with an SSD preferred, and Chromebooks are not accepted. A webcam, a good quality USB headset, and a quiet, distraction free home workspace complete the list.

For those who qualify, the trade-off is attractive: steady daytime hours, no commute, no transport costs, and income earned from home.

Applications go to [email protected], and the company stresses one important instruction: include your full name in the email subject line.

World.title: Guyana ferry captain charged with murder over 73 deaths
World.content:
Guyana ferry captain charged with murder over 73 deaths

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The MV Barima disaster has become a murder case. The captain and two crew members of the Guyanese passenger ferry that capsized with catastrophic loss of life were charged with murder on Tuesday, more than a week after the disaster killed 73 people and left 30 others still missing.

As reported by Reuters, Captain Kevin Price, 40, and crew members Rondell Dwayne Roberts, 42, and Delon Granderson, 33, appeared before a Georgetown court on the murder charges. They were not required to enter pleas, and the news agency could not immediately reach the defendants or their representatives for comment. The three were remanded to prison, with the case adjourned to August 3.

The charges attach to a tragedy whose dimensions have grown darker with each disclosure. The MV Barima, an 87-year-old ship, sank on July 18 while travelling from Georgetown to the northwestern village of Port Kaituma. Authorities say 76 passengers and crew were rescued, and believe 179 people were on board, far more than early reports indicated.

Prime Minister Mark Phillips has said that two of the crew members, including the captain, tested positive for marijuana following the accident, and that many of those on board had never been listed on the vessel’s passenger manifest. The Prime Minister maintained, however, that the vessel had been deemed seaworthy and had kept up with its maintenance schedule, an assertion the official inquiry will now test.

That inquiry carries a Belizean signature. President Irfaan Ali’s Commission of Inquiry into the disaster is chaired by Justice Godfrey Smith of Belize, the former Attorney General and CARICOM High-Level Representative for Law and Criminal Justice, leading an international panel empowered to determine whether negligence, misconduct, or institutional failures contributed to the tragedy. A wide-ranging investigation into the ferry services, run by the Transport and Harbours Department under the Ministry of Public Works, is also underway.

The political reckoning has begun in parallel. Opposition lawmakers have called for the resignations of Public Works Minister Juan Edghill and Public Utilities and Aviation Minister Deodat Indar.

As with any criminal matter, the three accused are presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty before the court.

For the families of the 73 recovered and the 30 still missing, Tuesday’s charges mark the first formal step toward accountability, with the deeper answers, how an 87-year-old ferry came to carry an uncounted crowd into disaster, resting with the courts and the Belizean-led commission. Breaking Belize News will continue to follow the case.

World.title: Security Guard fined $3,000 for drug trafficking after admitting he tried selling weed to support his parents
World.content:
Security Guard fined $3,000 for drug trafficking after admitting he tried selling weed to support his parents

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 28-year-old Belize City security guard avoided imprisonment on Tuesday after pleading guilty to drug trafficking involving 940 grams (a little over 2 pounds) of cannabis.

Barrington Earl Vanson was fined $3,000, along with $5 in court costs, and was given until December 30, 2026, to pay. If he fails to pay the fine by the deadline, he will serve one year in prison.

Vanson was arraigned in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Monday evening and pleaded guilty to possession of a controlled drug with intent to supply.

During his mitigation plea, Vanson admitted that he had attempted to sell the cannabis but claimed it was the first time he had become involved in selling drugs.

“I promise it won’t happen again because usually I do my little security work,” Vanson told the court. “I usually do handyman work too, chopping yards and cleaning garbage. I am asking for leniency.”

Vanson said he normally earns money through security and odd jobs but made the decision to sell cannabis because both of his parents were unemployed and he was trying to help support them.

“I know I messed up really big, and that was a stupid choice I made to survive because I have my ma to care for and my father. Both are not working right now,” he said. “I was just doing something on the side to help my family. This is the first time I decided to do this.”

The court imposed a non-custodial sentence after considering his guilty plea and mitigation.

According to police, at about 1:30 a.m. on Monday, July 27, members of the Violence Enforcement Team acted on information that cannabis was being kept inside Room No. 7 at a building located at the corner of Dean and Plues streets.

Officers visited the apartment and met Vanson, who identified himself as a security guard. Police informed him that they intended to search the premises for illegal firearms and ammunition and asked whether he had anything illegal to declare. He reportedly said no.

During the search, officers found a bag containing a grey plastic bag with seven smaller parcels of green, leafy material suspected to be cannabis.

Vanson was taken to the police station, where the substance was weighed in his presence and amounted to 940 grams.

This version keeps the court details while giving greater prominence to how Vanson normally earns a living and his explanation for committing the offence.

World.title: Collin Francis Jr. pleads guilty to manslaughter in Nestor Vasquez death and attempted murder in nurse stabbing
World.content:
Collin Francis Jr. pleads guilty to manslaughter in Nestor Vasquez death and attempted murder in nurse stabbing

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Collin Francis Jr. pleaded guilty in the High Court on Tuesday to manslaughter in the death of 60-year-old Nestor Vasquez and attempted murder in the stabbing of psychiatric nurse Augustina Elijio.

Justice Nigel Pilgrim accepted the pleas and scheduled sentencing for September 7, 2026, following mitigation. The court ordered a social inquiry report, prison report and victim impact statements in both cases.

Francis was initially charged with murder in Vasquez’s death, but the Crown accepted a manslaughter plea based on diminished responsibility. Medical records showed that Francis was experiencing an acute psychotic episode and had been diagnosed with schizophrenia at the time.

Elijio was attacked on June 4, 2019, at the Port Loyola Mental Health Clinic, where Francis had gone seeking treatment. She was stabbed in the right breast and rib cage, suffering injuries classified as grievous harm.

Two days later, while Francis was detained at the Queen Street Police Station, Vasquez was found badly beaten in a pool of blood inside the cell area. Vasquez died on June 8, 2019, from blunt-force traumatic injuries to the head.

Francis was previously deemed unfit to plead in 2024 and underwent psychiatric evaluations every six months. A recent evaluation found that he was stable while taking his medication and abstaining from marijuana.

He has been on remand since June 2019.

World.title: The Devil Made Me Do It: Jehovah’s Witness busted wearing tourist’s clothes after stealing his suitcase from bus
World.content:
The Devil Made Me Do It: Jehovah’s Witness busted wearing tourist’s clothes after stealing his suitcase from bus

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 36-year-old self-described Jehovah’s Witness was remanded to the Belize Central Prison after admitting that he stole a French tourist’s suitcase, wore some of the stolen clothing and sold other items because he wanted money to buy food.

Collin Burton Ramclam pleaded guilty to theft after admitting that he took the suitcase when he found it unattended on a bus travelling from Belmopan to Belize City.

The suitcase belonged to 20-year-old French national Ange Cesar Cirnevin, who reported it stolen on Friday, July 24.

Ramclam was later taken to the police station while wearing the tourist’s green polo shirt, a white, black and red scarf around his head and a silver Festina wristwatch valued at $300. Police also recovered the tourist’s grey suitcase and a bag containing clothing.

Ramclam reportedly told police, “I am sorry. I just meh wah money to buy food. I done sell the jeans pants and a wristwatch.”

Most of the property was recovered, except for one wristwatch and two pairs of jeans valued at $60.

In mitigation, Ramclam told the court that his own phone had been stolen the previous night, that he had been drinking and that he was hungry and had no money. He said a bus conductor had given him a free ride home from Belmopan after he travelled there to seek construction work.

Ramclam told the court that he fell asleep on the bus and noticed the suitcase when he awoke in Belize City. He admitted that he should have turned it over to the conductor but instead took it when he saw no one nearby.

The father of one asked the court for leniency, telling the magistrate that he attends Jehovah’s Witness services every Wednesday and Sunday and promising that the offence would not happen again.

Ramclam also admitted that he was not a first-time offender and had previously been convicted of theft in the Belmopan area. The senior magistrate remanded him while considering an appropriate sentence.

World.title: Belize’s Gonz Auto Stars crowned Champions at Copa Cancún Basketball Tournament
World.content:
Belize’s Gonz Auto Stars crowned Champions at Copa Cancún Basketball Tournament

By Zoila Palma: Belize’s Gonz Auto Stars returned home with championship honors after delivering an impressive performance at the XII Copa Cancún Basketball Tournament in Cancún, Quintana Roo, Mexico.

They competed with both its U15 and U17 teams from July 23 to 26, facing strong competition from teams across the region.

Both Gonz Auto Stars teams showcased determination, discipline and teamwork throughout the tournament, battling hard in every game and representing Belize with pride. Their performances reflected the commitment and fighting spirit that have become hallmarks of the Gonz Auto Stars basketball program.

The biggest achievement came from the U17 team, which captured first place to bring the championship title home to Belize. The victory was celebrated as a testament to the players’ hard work, dedication and belief in one another.

The team credited coaches Gabriel Taylor, Ronell Gonzalez Sr., Cordel Gonzalez Jr. and Cordel Gonzalez Sr. for their leadership, preparation and support throughout the tournament.

Gonz Auto Stars also expressed gratitude to its sponsors and everyone who supported the team’s BBQ fundraiser, which helped make the international trip possible.

World.title: Man remanded to prison after 10-year-old reports that 3-teeth man touched her inappropriately and gave her $3 not to tell anyone
World.content:
Man remanded to prison after 10-year-old reports that 3-teeth man touched her inappropriately and gave her $3 not to tell anyone

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Lords Bank resident accused of sexually assaulting a 10-year-old girl was remanded to the Belize Central Prison after the Belize City Magistrate’s Court denied his application for bail following detailed submissions from both the prosecution and defense.

Manuel De Jesus Flores, a local mason, appeared before a Senior Magistrate in Court #5 to face two counts of sexual assault. The charges allege that on July 18, 2026, Flores intentionally and unlawfully touched the female minor—who is 10 years and 5 months old—in a sexual manner without her consent.

The allegations stem from an incident occurring around 12:30 a.m. while the child’s mother was briefly away at a neighboring home. According to court details, the child reported that an elderly man standing at a construction site two lots over motioned for her to come to him. When she refused and went inside, he later entered her yard, asked for a hug, and grabbed her left hand when she attempted to walk away. The assailant then lifted her hips, pressed his erection against her body, touched her inappropriately, and squeezed her breast. Before releasing her, he handed her a $1 coin and a $2 bill, telling her not to tell anyone. The victim threw the money back at him, ran down the street carrying her younger cousin, and met her mother on the road to report what had occurred.

During court proceedings, defense attorney Sharon Pitts-Robateau made extensive submissions advocating for her client’s release, seeking bail even after the sitting Magistrate initially indicated a denial due to the grave nature of the offense. Attorney Pitts highlighted that Flores is gainfully employed as a mason and emphasized the fundamental presumption of innocence, pointing out that the charges are strictly allegations at this stage. She argued that the essential legal purpose of bail is to ensure a defendant returns to court, a goal that could be achieved by setting strict bail conditions rather than remanding him.

Police Prosecutor Sgt. Ayala vigorously countered the application, urging the Senior Magistrate to consider several key factors against granting release. Sgt. Ayala cited the very young age of the victim, the high prevalence and seriousness of sexual assault offenses, and the likelihood that Flores might reoffend given the early morning hour of the alleged incident. The prosecution further argued that releasing the accused would present a significant risk of interference with the young victim or the ongoing police investigation.

After considering the arguments from both sides, the Senior Magistrate sustained the prosecution’s objections and refused bail. Flores was remanded in custody to the Belize Central Prison until his next scheduled court appearance on September 17, 2026.

World.title: Central Bank of Belize, FIU and Financial Services Commission sign Governance Agreements for use of Sanctions Registry
World.content:
Central Bank of Belize, FIU and Financial Services Commission sign Governance Agreements for use of Sanctions Registry

By Zoila Palma: The Central Bank of Belize (the Central Bank), the Financial Intelligence Unit (FIU), and the Financial Services Commission (FSC) have signed governance agreements establishing the framework for the shared use of the Sanctions Registry System (SRS).

A joint statement explained that SRS is a secure supervisory platform developed by the Central Bank, and designed to support the management of sanctions-related information and strengthen Belize’s framework for combatting money laundering, terrorist financing, and other forms of financial crime. By improving information management, data retrieval, and analytical capability, the system enables a more efficient, consistent, and risk-based approach to supervision.

“The governance agreements provide the legal and operational framework for participating authorities to access and use the SRS in support of their respective statutory responsibilities. While each institution will utilise the system independently within its own supervisory environment, the shared platform promotes greater consistency in regulatory information management and enhances opportunities for collaboration where appropriate,” it added.

The initiative reflects the continued commitment of the Central Bank, the FIU, and the FSC to strengthening inter-agency cooperation through the effective use of technological innovation, improved information sharing, and modern supervisory practices.

The Central Bank, FIU, and FSC said that they remain committed to working collaboratively to strengthen Belize’s regulatory framework, enhance supervisory effectiveness, and promote a safe, sound and resilient financial system.
