The actual figure may differ, but we should be working step by step to reduce the foreign stake and increase our own.

“The Russian state-owned company effectively holds a monopoly in Georgia, as it controls electricity generation, distribution and supply. This is not just a business issue—it also concerns political and strategic interests. When a neighbouring and unpredictable state owns your strategic assets, it creates long-term macroeconomic risks.

“At the same time, these companies generate relatively modest annual profits compared with their capital—around 3%—which suggests that, for Russia, these assets are more a tool of political influence than a source of economic gain.”

Inter RAO and Georgia’s Energy Sector

World.title: US Embassy expresses concern over creation of Georgia’s hate speech unit
World.content:
The US Embassy in Georgia says it is concerned by the creation of a new hate speech unit, according to a written response to a request from Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty.

The unit was established under the Ministry of Internal Affairs and began operating on 1 June 2026. According to the official description, it is responsible for “monitoring and taking legal action in response to hate speech, abusive campaigns and aggressive communication in the public sphere.”

The embassy stressed that the administration of President Donald Trump and the United States regard freedom of speech as a fundamental pillar of a functioning society and strongly oppose censorship.

Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty sent its request to the US Embassy on 22 July, after journalist Vakho Sanaia was sentenced to 14 days in administrative detention over a Facebook post insulting members of the ruling Georgian Dream party — Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili and MP Vlado Bozhadze.

What the embassy said

“The Donald Trump administration has made it clear that the United States views freedom of speech as a fundamental pillar of a functioning society, and we strongly oppose censorship and restrictive laws used to silence people whose views are deemed undesirable.

As we have shared with our Georgian partners, stability requires a political opposition that engages with state institutions on behalf of the citizens who elected it. Political stability, underpinned by broad representation of different views, is among the factors that make Georgia a reliable partner for US investment, security cooperation and a long-term strategic partnership.

We are concerned by the Georgian government’s creation of a hate speech unit. The best response to falsehoods and misguided views is more free speech, not enforced silence.”

Georgia’s hate speech unit

World.title: Abkhazia to buy Russian electricity ‘just in case’ from August to November
World.content:
The state-owned energy company Chernomorenergo plans to import electricity from Russia into Abkhazia between August and November to preserve water levels in the Jvar reservoir, which supplies the Ingur hydropower plant.

Until now, electricity imports took place only during the winter months, when water levels at the plant dropped. However, as electricity prices are significantly higher during that period, the Abkhaz authorities have decided to stock up on electricity while it is cheaper.

The 40% share of electricity generated by the Inguri hydropower plant allocated to Abkhazia under an informal agreement reached after the 1992–93 Georgian-Abkhaz war has, over the past decade, proved insufficient to meet the republic’s electricity needs.

According to Chernomorenergo Director General Timur Dzhindzholia, the annual shortfall amounts to around 500–650 million kWh. While Abkhazia’s budget now includes funding for electricity imports, it is not enough to fully cover the deficit. As a result, the government has opted to purchase Russian electricity during the months when prices are at their lowest.

As recently as two years ago, largely because of uncontrolled cryptocurrency mining, electricity consumption in Abkhazia reached 3 billion kWh a year. During the autumn and winter months, the republic experienced rolling blackouts.

A series of measures to optimise electricity consumption has significantly reduced the deficit. In 2025, around 320 million kWh was covered by humanitarian electricity supplies from Russia, while the remaining shortfall had to be met through commercial imports.

Timur Dzhindzholia said that eliminating the deficit entirely would require the construction of new power generation facilities.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Electricity imports from Russia to Abkhazia

World.title: Study finds women in Armenia work more hours than men because of unpaid household work
World.content:
Women in Armenia work more than men, study finds

Women in Armenia work roughly four to five times more than men on unpaid household and care responsibilities, according to a study conducted by Ameria for the Armenian office of the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA). The study found that women spend an average of 15.3 hours a week on household chores, including cooking, cleaning and laundry. They also devote another 8.6 hours to childcare, caring for elderly family members and other family responsibilities.

According to economist Tigran Jrbashyan, head of management consulting at Ameria, women aged 30 to 35 carry the heaviest workload. They spend between 44 and 49 hours a week on these responsibilities.

“This is unpaid labour. No one pays for it. Yet by doing this work, women create value. That is extremely important and deserves recognition,” Jrbashyan said.

By comparison, men spend an average of less than four hours (3.6) a week on household chores. They devote just over two hours (2.2) to caring for family members. Men aged 30 to 40 record the highest figures, spending between eight and 11 hours a week.

Women receive no pay for 78% of the work they do

The researchers found that women in Armenia spend more time on various activities than men. Much of that time goes to household responsibilities, placing a heavier physical burden on them. Yet no one pays them for caring for their families.

According to Tigran Jrbashyan, women receive no pay for 78% of the work they do, as household responsibilities account for that share of their overall workload.

“In effect, women receive pay for only 22% of the work they do. For men, unpaid work accounts for around 11%, while paid work makes up the remaining 89%.”

‘It is important to make workplaces more family-friendly’

Lusine Sargsyan, head of the Yerevan office of the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), says that spending 44 to 49 hours a week on unpaid household work often forces women to make a choice: whether to enter the workforce, whether to prioritise their careers or focus on starting a family and having children.

“We need to create conditions where women no longer have to choose one or the other. They should be able to have both. It is important that women can pursue formal employment while also having time for their families. Otherwise, the country will face demographic challenges,” she said.

When Sargsyan talks about creating better conditions for working women, she refers in particular to expanding access to nurseries and kindergartens, as well as developing childcare centres for young children.

Remote work is already available in Armenia, and working mothers can take advantage of it with their employer’s consent. The government has also recently introduced a “parental hour” policy. Under the new rules, working parents with children under the age of 12 can either arrive at work later or leave earlier. Parents with one or two children can reduce their working day by 30 minutes. Those with three or more children can shorten it by one hour. However, experts say these measures do not go far enough to create a truly family-friendly working environment.

Lusine Sargsyan stresses that spending 44 to 49 hours a week on household responsibilities means some women effectively work two full-time jobs. In addition to unpaid domestic work, they spend another 40 hours a week working for an employer.

She argues that this is problematic both economically and from a human rights perspective because women are left with little or no time for themselves. She also says excessive workloads reduce productivity at work and affect the quality of care they can provide for their children at home.

Sargsyan emphasises that workplaces need to become more family-friendly. That would allow women to fulfil their potential while also spending meaningful time with their families.

“Employers need to recognise that their employees have families. It is extremely important that women do not live with a constant sense of guilt. They should not feel guilty about spending too little time with their families. Nor should they worry at home about work they did not finish,” she explained.

Both Sargsyan and Jrbashyan stressed that many women are highly productive and, in many cases, better educated than men.

They argue that the country needs to create better conditions for women to work. Otherwise, the economy risks missing out on the higher value they could generate.

At the same time, both experts stressed that they are not arguing every woman should have formal employment or receive pay for household work. Instead, they say women should have the freedom to decide how they want to organise their lives. They believe giving women that choice would benefit the country’s economy, improve business performance and create a healthier family environment.

Women in Armenia work more than men, study finds

World.title: GYLA: ‘Georgia has effectively created an informal ‘morality police’, which could become a new form of violence’
World.content:
GYLA warns violence could escalate in Georgia

The Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association (GYLA) has responded to reports about the creation of a movement to protect traditional values, warning that alongside existing legal restrictions on freedom of expression, assembly and civic participation, the initiative could introduce new mechanisms of violence in the country.

The movement was announced on 26 July by MMA fighter Giorgi Kartvelishvili and several supporters. At a press briefing, he said the organisation would “respond immediately” to issues involving the country’s ancestors, religion, history and other subjects that the group considers offensive. Kartvelishvili said the movement would be “highly active, respectable and constructive”, adding that any “patriotic Georgian” would be welcome to join. Members of the group also said they were prepared to take responsibility for their actions, including serving prison sentences if necessary.

GYLA described the initiative as the creation of an informal “morality police”, warning that it poses a threat to freedom of expression in Georgia.

According to the organisation, “everything suggests that the group’s aim may be to informally monitor, intimidate or pressure people who are critical of the authorities.”

GYLA’s lawyers added that “attempts to establish vigilante groups in the country are particularly alarming” given the rise in violence and intimidation targeting government critics in recent years.

GYLA said members of the new group are using defamatory and disinformation-laden language that closely mirrors narratives promoted by the authorities and pro-government media.

In particular, the group says it is launching a campaign “against people and organisations funded from abroad, enslaved to foreign interests and driven by a perverse ideology.”

According to GYLA, the group’s statements contain signs of incitement to violence. The lawyers pointed in particular to its declaration that “if circumstances leave no alternative, members of the group will not be afraid of going to prison.”

GYLA said the group has already demanded an apology from stand-up comedian Onise Okriashvili, who was recently severely beaten in the street after making a joke referring to Georgian literary classic Nodar Dumbadze.

The group has also asked prosecutors not to seek a prison sentence for the person accused of attacking Okriashvili. Otherwise, its representatives warned, there could be reprisals, according to GYLA.

“We will hold people accountable for every action and comment that insults the dignity of the Georgian people,” the group said in a statement cited by GYLA.

GYLA said such statements echo remarks made by senior officials from the ruling Georgian Dream party which, in the organisation’s view, call for greater control over freedom of expression.

The organisation also noted that attacks by third parties targeting people critical of the government were widely documented during the 2024 protests and in the months that followed.

According to GYLA, such incidents were often accompanied by statements from state officials appearing to support the attackers or by an inadequate response from law enforcement.

“Against this background, it is clear that the creation of a vigilante group and its declared intention to police citizens’ freedom of expression are closely linked to the state’s ongoing normalisation of violence,” GYLA said.

The organisation noted that Georgian criminal law prohibits the creation, leadership or membership of illegal armed or violent groups. It also bans the establishment of associations, or participation in them, if their activities involve violence against individuals.

GYLA said law enforcement authorities must take all measures provided for by law to prevent violence or intimidation against people exercising their fundamental rights.

According to the organisation, “pro-government media are actively contributing to the demonisation and targeting of individuals, which may amount to incitement to violence and complicity in it. The inaction or delayed response of state institutions creates an environment that enables violence to spread.”

GYLA warns violence could escalate in Georgia

World.title: Georgian banks to continue servicing local subsidiaries of sanctioned Russian energy giant Inter RAO
World.content:
Georgian banks to continue servicing Telasi

The National Bank of Georgia has announced that the country’s commercial banks will continue providing services in the national currency to Telasi, despite the company being owned by Russian energy giant Inter RAO, which was included in the European Union’s latest, 21st package of sanctions against Russia. The central bank confirmed the decision to BM.GE.

At the end of July, the European Union imposed sanctions on the Russian state-controlled energy company Inter RAO. Through its subsidiaries, the company is the indirect owner of Georgia’s electricity distribution companies Telasi and Telmiko, as well as the Khramhesi-1 and Khramhesi-2 hydropower plants.

The National Bank said that Telasi itself is not included on any sanctions list and that its uninterrupted operation is essential for the country’s population and economy. According to the central bank, while compliance with international sanctions is important, it is equally crucial to ensure the uninterrupted provision of essential services to the public.

The National Bank said that each sanctions-related case would be assessed on its individual merits. As a result, banks will continue providing services to Telasi “in compliance with the applicable sanctions regime, as well as in accordance with their own internal policies and risk assessment procedures.”

Georgian banks to continue servicing Telasi

World.title: Former political staffer settles case over Brittany Higgins fallout
World.content:
The former political staffer to whom Brittany Higgins first disclosed her rape allegation has settled a contentious lawsuit with the Commonwealth over claims her workplace rights were compromised in the fallout of the controversy.

Fiona Brown was the chief of staff for former Liberal senator Linda Reynolds in 2019 when Ms Higgins claimed she was sexually assaulted by her fellow staffer Bruce Lehrmann.

The veteran public servant became a central figure in the scandal and the defamation trial that followed over claims she had been party to a Liberal government "cover-up" of the assault.

Ms Higgins alleged the rape occurred in Ms Reynolds's ministerial office, but the matter did not become public knowledge until 2021.

Bruce Lehrmann was later arrested and faced a trial in the ACT Supreme Court, but it collapsed with no criminal findings against him.

While the Federal Court found in April 2024 that Ms Higgins was, on the balance of probabilities, raped in Senator Reynolds's office, it did not accept claims that the government or Ms Brown had engaged in concealing the assault.

Mr Lehrmann continues to maintain his innocence.

Brittany Higgins disclosed her rape allegation to Fiona Brown, who was chief of staff to Senator Linda Reynolds at the time. (AAP Image: Richard Wainwright)

Claims then-PM froze her out

Nearly a year after those findings, Ms Brown lodged a Fair Work case in the Federal Court, claiming that her workplace rights were breached and that she was effectively made a fall-person for the government as it scrambled to respond to the story.

Part of her case centred on a tense Question Time in the days after the allegations, when then-prime minister Scott Morrison faced a barrage of questions about Ms Higgins's story from then-opposition leader Anthony Albanese.

Ms Brown claimed Mr Morrison had falsely told parliament that he had spoken with her about Ms Higgins when he had not, and said the former prime minister had refused to talk to her after the story broke, except to tell her that they had discussed the matter.

The veteran public servant told the court she had felt frightened and intimidated by the interaction.

Ms Brown also claimed she was falsely framed to take the responsibility in February 2022, when Mr Morrison made a national apology to Ms Higgins over her mistreatment.

She also claimed she was subsequently stripped of key responsibilities and Mr Morrison's advisors had stopped her from responding to media questions to publicly defend her actions.

The Commonwealth rejected the claim that it had harmed Ms Brown.

Fiona Brown said an interaction with former prime minister Scott Morrison left her feeling intimidated. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

The Fair Work case had been scheduled to head to a trial next March, which was set to last more than three weeks with Mr Morrison among the expected witnesses.

Instead, Ms Brown and the Commonwealth resolved the matter through a mediation process earlier this month.

A spokesperson for Federal Attorney-General Michelle Rowland said it noted an agreement had been reached, but did not specify any financial sum.

"It would be inappropriate to make any further comment at this time due to privacy considerations, legal professional privilege and confidentiality obligations," the spokesperson said.

The Federal Court is still yet to formally sign off on the agreed settlement.

The ABC has contacted Ms Brown's lawyers for comment.

World.title: One Nation asked to submit three years of missing financial statements
World.content:
One Nation has vowed to hand in three years' worth of tardy accounts that have threatened to see the political party's hometown entity cancelled by regulators.

The vow comes after the Office of Fair Trading (OFT) confirmed that One Nation Queensland Division Inc had until midway through next month to file audited accounts for the financial years from 2023 to 2025.

"One Nation is complying with the Office of Fair Trading's requirements, which have requested we lodge audited financial statements by 18 August 2026," a party spokesman told the ABC.

How One Nation is winning over the bush One Nation has some of its strongest support in outback Australia and recent polling shows it could win over 30 regional seats. So what's winning over regional Australians when it comes to Pauline Hanson's party?

One Nation, founded by Pauline Hanson in 1997 in Queensland, has surged in polls this year to emerge as a potential key threat to mainstream political parties.

But scrutiny is intensifying with accounts being late with the Queensland division, which also is listed on Australian business registers as the holder of trading names including One Nation, Pauline Hanson's One Nation and Young Nation.

Senator Hanson is president of the division, according to her register of interests.

The Queensland division is registered in the state as an incorporated association, but it had failed to supply annual records as required, which legislation indicates is six months after the end of a financial year.

The OFT had now sought the Queensland division to hand these in audited statements. (ABC News: Briana Fiore)

The state's Office of Fair Trading confirmed that the division had now lodged its annual returns for the three financial years to 2025 "but these returns did not include the audited financial statements as required".

The OFT had now sought the Queensland division to hand these in audited statements.

If the division fails to hand in the statements, the OFT can instigate an investigation.

Any negative findings could result in infringement notices and small fines against committee members or even the issuing of a show cause notice about why the association's incorporation should not be cancelled.

One Nation's spokesman did not answer why the accounts had not been filed on time.

World.title: Family embroiled in decades-old IVF mix-up files lawsuit against hospital
World.content:
The biological parents of twins who were born after an IVF embryo mix-up at Royal North Shore Hospital in Sydney have launched a civil claim in the NSW Supreme Court against the facility.

Last year, Sasha Szafranski and her twin sister accidentally discovered they had been born to a woman who was not their biological parent, after a mix-up at a fertility clinic within the hospital.

The embryo mix-up occurred in 1995 and the twins were raised by their birth mother without either family being aware of what had occurred.

The mix-up When Sasha Szafranski matched with a stranger on a genealogy website, she uncovered an IVF mix-up that had been hidden for 30 years.

Now the biological parents have taken legal action.

Lawyers acting for Jacqueline and Richard Hensby-Davies, have told the ABC that a statement of claim has been issued against Royal North Shore Hospital.

"Our clients were hopeful that a formal apology and compensation could be negotiated without the need for issue of court proceedings," Bill Madden and Matilda Lynch of Carroll and O'Dea Lawyers said.

"However, as the matter is complex that could not be achieved and so a statement of claim has now been filed in relation to the IVF error."

The lawyers added that the provision of care also involved another organisation and "investigations are continuing as to whether another defendant or defendants should be added to the claim".

Family left without answers after discovering embryo mix-up

The embryo mix-up only came to light when Ms Szafranski tried to learn more about her father's family by sending her DNA away for testing through the website Ancestry.com.

Ms Szafranski told her story to the ABC in March, detailing her confusing DNA results and the eventual match she found with a woman she later learned was her biological aunt.

Further independent DNA testing showed Ms Szafranski and her twin sister were the biological children of Richard and Jacqueline Hensby-Davies, a couple who lived a 15-minute drive away from the childhood home of the twins in Coffs Harbour.

Investigations by the families showed that the Hensby-Davieses and the twins' birth mother, Penny Szafranski, underwent IVF treatment at Royal North Shore Hospital's fertility clinic at the same time in 1995.

Ms Szafranski fell pregnant at that time, but Ms Hensby-Davies did not.

Sasha Szafranski shared her family's story with the ABC in March. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

In March, the Northern Sydney Local Health District, which controls Royal North Shore Hospital, said the hospital's fertility unit was transferred to a company called North Shore A.R.T in August 1994.

The health district said it "did not operate the clinic after this time".

August 1994 was eight months before the mistaken embryo transfer to Penny Szafranski occurred.

North Shore A.R.T no longer exists and was acquired in the early 2000s by another company, which was later acquired by IVF giant Virtus Health.

Earlier this year, a spokesperson for Virtus Health strongly denied it was responsible, saying the incident occurred before the company was established.

"In 1995, Virtus Health did not own or operate any entity associated with this incident," the spokesperson said.

That stalemate meant both families were left to deal with a life-changing discovery, without any understanding of how the embryo mix-up occurred.

This case is Australia's second-known instance of an IVF embryo mix-up where an embryo was transferred to the wrong family, and one of a series of incidents that has raised broader concerns about regulation in the sector.

Earlier this year, fertility giant Monash IVF agreed to pay financial settlements to families involved in two major bungles — including the other known case of a wrong embryo being transferred between families, which occurred in Monash's Brisbane clinic in 2023.

The second case involved a woman's own embryo being incorrectly transferred to her, instead of her partner's embryo, at Monash's Melbourne facilities.

Monash is facing further legal action in relation to the Brisbane case from a third couple who believed their embryos had been provided for the Brisbane mother to give birth.

Daughter welcomes litigation, hopes it leads to change

Sasha Szafranski is not part of any litigation regarding her case.

She told the ABC she did not want to comment on the case that had been brought by her biological parents, but said she hoped it would lead to change in the IVF sector.

"What I do hope comes from this is accountability, transparency and meaningful change," she said.

"My hope has always been that no other person or family has to experience what ours has.

"I also ask that everyone involved is treated with compassion, this has been deeply personal for all of us and there are many people carrying enormous pain."

The Northern Sydney Local Health District declined to comment.

World.title: Major police incident blocks main road in Adelaide's north
World.content:
A major police operation is underway in Adelaide's north, where emergency services have cordoned off a section of main road at Elizabeth East.

Dozens of police are at the scene and Main North Road is blocked to southbound traffic from Midway Road.

While details are unclear, police are expected to provide an update at a media conference this afternoon.

There is a major presence by emergency services, and at least 12 police cars are parked at the scene.

Police have cordoned off an area with several hundred metres of tape stretching from the centre of the road to a nature reserve next to the Playford City Tennis Centre.

Main North Road has been partially blocked amid a major police operation. (ABC News: Lincoln Rothall)

In a Facebook post, SA Police said it was responding to an incident near the intersection of Fairfield Road.

"Southbound traffic on Main North Road is blocked and will be diverted. Members of the public are to be guided by police at diversion points," it said.

Firefighters are assisting police, and a Metropolitan Fire Service incident command vehicle and truck have attended.

World.title: Japanese mall had just reopened before earthquake and explosion
World.content:
The Japanese mall where a deadly explosion struck after Tuesday's earthquake had only just reopened last month, after undergoing repairs to damage caused in a devastating earthquake a decade ago.

Live blog: Get the latest updates on the Japan earthquake

Thirteen people have now been confirmed dead after a magnitude-7.1 earthquake hit Japan's southern Kumamoto Prefecture on Tuesday, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said.

"Even now, there are people waiting to be rescued, and this is a race against time," she told reporters at her office in Tokyo.

About 200 people were evacuated from the Aeon Kumamoto mall following the quake.

About an hour later, an explosion ripped through the shopping complex, causing ceilings and walls to collapse and trapping several people inside.

At least two women, both in their 20s, died in the mall disaster, Japan's Fire and Disaster Management Agency told news agency Agence France-Presse (AFP).

A gas leak was suspected to be the cause of the blast at the mall, a government source told the Kyodo news agency.

The shopping complex was badly damaged in the earthquake. (Kyodo via Reuters)

"The explosion occurred after the customers and staff had evacuated," a spokesman for the mall's operator Aeon told AFP.

A local official told AFP that eight people had been rescued from the mall, five of them with injuries.

Initial reports suggested about 20 to 30 people could have been trapped inside the building, but the public broadcaster cited police saying the number was lower than that.

They added the exact number was not known, and emergency services had not yet found a safe route to enter the building.

Emergency workers inspecting the damaged Aeon Mall shopping centre. (Reuters: Kim Kyung-Hoon)

According to Kyodo, about 200 people had been evacuated from the mall after the earthquake.

Authorities said the second floor of the building had collapsed.

A fresh start turned to rubble

It was meant to be a fresh start for the Aeon Kumamoto mall as it reopened its doors on June 13.

It had undergone extensive repairs after it was damaged in the magnitude-7.3 earthquake that hit Kumamoto in 2016 and claimed the lives of 270 people.

According to Reuters, the mall was so badly damaged that it had to ​close for months and be rebuilt over even longer periods.

During a 2017 redevelopment, the mall highlighted its seismically reinforced ceilings and overall improvements to safety and ⁠resilience.

It housed some 200 stores and businesses and a cinema, and it had ​room for 5,000 cars in its parking lot.

On Tuesday, much of the sprawling site was reduced to a skeleton and rubble.

In ​Japan's smaller cities, Aeon's malls ​are often vibrant sites ⁠for shopping and entertainment.

"As we mark both the 21st year since opening and the 10th anniversary of the region's recovery [from the 2016 earthquake], we are undertaking a major renewal of the shopping centre," Aeon Kumamoto had said in a ⁠press release ​to commemorate the event in mid-June.

"Through this 're-start' initiative, we will embark on a ​new stage of growth and strive to become a shopping centre that brings enjoyment to customers throughout the region."

Loading...

ABC/Reuters/AFP

World.title: Motorists to lose fuel discount from Monday
World.content:
Drivers will lose their fuel discount from Monday after the government officially confirmed the fuel excise relief will end as planned, despite escalating pressure on global oil prices due to the war in Iran.

The original 50 per cent discount, which knocked 32 cents off each litre of petrol, was dropped back to 16 cents from July and is scheduled to end on August 2.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers said it was "never the government's intention" to make the scheme permanent.

"The fuel excise relief will end at midnight on Sunday," he said.

"It has played a really important role helping to take some of the sting out of the cost-of-living pressures.

"It was never the government's intention for that to be permanent."

Track the latest petrol and diesel prices around Australia See what's happening with petrol and diesel prices near you, updated constantly.

He said the discount was being binned at the start of the month "deliberately" to create a smooth downward taper from its original relief of 32 cents.

The Heavy Vehicle Road User Charge discount will also end on Monday.

Last week oil prices crept over $US100 a barrel for the first time since May. It dipped back down to $US86.36 a barrel on Wednesday.

It comes amid a fresh escalation in the conflict between the United States and Iran as a memorandum of understanding between the two has unravelled.

Treasury warns world has 'weaker buffers'

The confirmation comes despite a warning from Treasury that the world had depleted reserves and had "weaker buffers" to absorb ongoing disruptions to oil supply.

In a briefing note seen by the ABC, Treasury said the spread of the conflict into the Red Sea, an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, as well as Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries, had damaged global resilience.

Treasury war impact warning The federal government is yet to reveal whether it will extend the fuel excise discount, which is set to expire this week.

"During the initial phase of the conflict the energy price shock, although significant, was contained … [including by] re-routing of exports, a drawdown in oil inventories, and some demand destruction," the briefing notes stated.

"The oil market is now more vulnerable. These factors mean that crude oil prices are likely to remain elevated in the near term.

"Upside risks to oil prices will build if the status quo persists. Price pressures may intensify over coming months."

On Saturday, Energy Minister Chris Bowen said Australians could be confident that supplies were stable.

Australia currently has 42 days of petrol, 38 days of diesel, and 32 days of jet fuel in stockpile.

World.title: 'Vasectomy at 21 and no regrets': Men on choosing to be childfree
World.content:
An increasing number of Australian men are choosing to be childfree, and climate change, financial concerns and prioritising adventure are some of the reasons readers shared with us.

We heard from child-free men after publishing our story on why more men are turning away from fatherhood.

Here is some of what some of them had to say.

Financial concerns

My choice to be childless is much the same as described in [your] article — fears of passing on my own mental health issues, seeing how having kids impacted my father's life negatively, and barely being able to afford to keep myself afloat, let alone the added cost of kids.

My brother had three kids and it's more important to me to be an additional safe adult in those kids' lives. If I had my own kids, I wouldn't be able to dedicate as much time or effort to have a relationship with them.

— David (not his real name), 34, Melbourne/Naarm

Sign up to the ABC Lifestyle newsletter Get a mid-week boost and receive easy recipes, wellbeing ideas, and home and garden tips in your inbox every Wednesday. You’ll also receive a monthly newsletter of our best recipes.

A hostile world

It doesn't feel responsible to have a child in a world where it's actively hostile to children or parents for existing.

The world not only has gotten more expensive there is also climate change, political instability, social media, wealth inequality, AI, [and] hostile government to consider.

There is nothing anyone can do can change my mind unless I see the world around me change into a more empathetic world.

— Jason (not his real name), 26, Adelaide/Tarntanya

I think I probably started telling people when I was a very young boy that I didn't want kids as an act of defiance.

As I grew into my teens, the big wide world penetrated my psyche: 9/11, the Iraq war, the encroaching gloom of 21st century living and ultimately climate change became important considerations. Was it really responsible to bring a child into this?

I have nieces and nephews and they are great, but when spending time with them, that deep primal longing for one of my own simply isn't there.

I ask my friends and colleagues about their reasons for having kids and there just never seems to be a compelling enough reason to venture down that path.

It feels like whatever society we're currently in is in the death throes of its life. No child should have to live through whatever is coming next.

— Steve (not his real name), aged in his 30s, north Queensland

Choosing adventure

From a young age, I felt having children was not for me. Even my father said I shouldn't have kids.

Why more men are choosing to be childfree About 15 per cent of Australian men say they don't want children, an increase from 11 per cent in 2005. Ian says his own childhood played a large part in his decision.

I think he saw an independent side in my nature, which only grew stronger as I got older.

As an adult, I have lived a life as an artist and traveller, full of creativity, spontaneity and adventure.

It was clear to me that I could only have this life if I remained childfree.

Raising children takes a lot of time, money and endless amounts of sacrifice, commitment, love and devotion. Rather than being a bad or less committed parent, I made the choice of not having a family.

Because I preferred to remain childfree, that added a major constraint for prospective partners. But even with this, I have no regrets.

— Raymond, aged in his 60s, Hobart/Nipaluna

I had vasectomy at 21. I do not and have not regretted this decision.

I am not huge fan of children.

I have been married to a wonderful woman for 30 years who feels the same way as I do.

We have lived a carefree and adventurous life and [have had] opportunities that would not be possible for families without big dollars.

— Jarod (not his real name), aged in his 50s, Tasmania

The stigma of being childfree

I have experienced the raising of eyebrows many times as if I have committed a sin or lacking some kind of capability of commitment.

At my previous job my manager told me I could be more patient and that I was not because I don't have a child.

I get a lot of comments from my friends that compare my dogs to children as if we have them because we can't have children. I have explained to them many times that I love dogs and I would have them regardless of having or not having a child.

I think my wife is under more pressure than me since everyone we visit is constantly talking about the magnificent and unique experience of giving birth and raising a child.

The difference between childfree and childless While not everyone in the childless or childfree communities will identify the same way, understanding the difference means we can respond more thoughtfully when learning about someone's parental status.

— Jack (not his real name), 46, Melbourne/Naarm

My wife and I are childfree.

My decision comes down to finances, patience, and political and environmental factors.

I've been asked by other men about my decision, which has had mixed responses of "Good for you" and more judgemental "What's wrong with you?"

— Zachary, 36, Brisbane/Meanjin

Leaving a legacy

My wife and I decided many years ago not to have children. It is not due to money, but time. We both work very long hours, and I have eight staff.

Strangely enough though, we do both long to pass something on, to leave a legacy, and are therefore keen to teach young people lessons we think are important.

My greatest fear of this choice though is that when I pass away, there will be nothing left of me for my wife physically. There will be money, but no semblance left of me in a child's face.

Friends with kids often have some degree of envy when looking at our material assets and the presumption of available time, and we look enviously at the way their kids look at and feel about them, but the truth is we have just as little time as they do.

— Rob, 47, Brisbane/Meanjin

Thank you to everyone who wrote to us about being childfree. Some comments have been edited for clarity and brevity.

World.title: Not-for-profits 'devastated' by council's planned $14m land sell-off
World.content:
Not-for-profit groups on the NSW South Coast say they are "devastated' by a plan to uproot their services as part of a $14 million council land deal.

The Shoalhaven City Council has narrowly voted to rezone and sell the land which is currently used by a children's disability service, a crisis housing shelter and a local youth hub.

The sites are among more than 20 properties it hopes to sell in a bid to raise money and stave off a potential rate rise for residents.

The affected groups include the Ulladulla-based children's disability service Noah's Inclusion Services.

CEO of Noah's Inclusion Services Alice Lans addressing Shoalhaven City Council on Tuesday evening. (ABC Illawarra: Charles Rushforth )

Addressing a public forum before a council meeting yesterday, Noah's CEO Alice Lans said she only became aware of the proposal when council business papers were released late last week.

"To receive this news at 5pm on Thursday was an unexpected and devastating blow," she said.

" Once a community asset like this is lost it cannot easily be replaced. "

Community land for sale

The Nowra Youth Centre and crisis homeless accommodation service Safe Shelter Shoalhaven operate on land currently classified for community use.

The council hopes to rezone the properties as part of the sale plan.

Safe Shelter Shoalhaven has capacity for 12 people experiencing homelessness and includes a community garden. (Supplied: Salt Care)

Safe Shelter Shoalhaven offers emergency overnight accommodation in Nowra for people experiencing homelessness, accommodating around 4,000 people a year.

The 12-bedroom shelter run by Salt Care is the only service of its kind in a town where more than 900 people are currently on waitlists for social housing.

CEO Peter Dover said he was fielding about 10 phone calls a day from concerned clients, employees and community members since the motion was announced last week.

"The community are saying, 'what's going on?'" he said.

Mr Dover said he was advised about the potential sale two months ago and received assurances from the council about assistance to relocate.

He said planning for a new shelter had not started.

"Planning needs to start now if there's going to be a new venue because it takes a long time to get things up and running," Mr Dover said.

" We need to assure the community that there is a plan and there is a way forward and that the homeless people of the Shoalhaven haven't been forgotten. "

Andrew Constance apologises

Mayor Patricia White introduced the land sale motion to councillors at a general meeting on Tuesday evening, describing it as a necessary measure to stave off an extraordinary rate rise.

"As far as I'm concerned the homeless services are a state issue," she said.

"We get no support, no subsidies from the state or federal government in helping us maintain these facilities.

"When they fall down because we can't go and fix them what are we going to do?"

Shoalhaven City Council Mayor Patricia White and CEO Andrew Constance. (ABC Illawarra: Charles Rushforth)

Questions about the size and complexity of the motion by councillors prompted CEO Andrew Constance to apologise, acknowledging local not-for-profits had not been consulted about the plan.

"I want to publicly apologise to Noah's," Mr Constance said.

" We got it wrong. "

Mr Constance promised the council would honour any existing leases and work to find replacement facilities in the future.

"We have to ensure that we work closely with our tenants to now go and do the necessary consultation … and work to provide better premises," he said.

The Nowra Youth Centre is one of several parcels of community land the council is planning to sell. (ABC Illawarra: Charles Rushforth)

Speaking in favour of the motion, Deputy Mayor Peter Wilkins said the land sale was a necessary evil.

"We live in difficult times and the council is affected, we have to share the pain," he said.

"And sharing that pain means land sales."

Councillor Gemma Tribe refuted that argument.

"The pain is being unfairly shared by the most vulnerable in our community," she said.

"Any money you hope to recoup from this will be lost in helping services to relocate.

" Is that really what you want your legacy to be? Displacing community groups from community land and doing a fire sale of community assets? "

South Coast MP Liza Butler outside the Shoalhaven City Council meeting chambers. (ABC Illawarra: Charles Rushforth)

Speaking after the meeting, South Coast Labor MP Liza Butler called on the community to oppose the plan.

"They've put forward a plan for [the sale of] a car park in Berry to be deferred, but not for these vital community services," she said.

"I hope the community really tells the council how they feel about this, because those services are vital."

World.title: Victorian Labor leadership LIVE: Ben Carroll faces SRL scrutiny as MPs are booted in rowdy question time

World.title: After controversy and conspiracy, can Drag Race Down Under win over the world?
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A



But the franchise is now back, back again, with a serious glow-up for its fifth season. This is the first of a “vs the World” spin-off, where five of Australia and New Zealand’s finest queens face off against international all-stars from the United States, Britain, Spain and the Philippines. “I’m excited! It’s a bigger production,” says Nicholson of the series, which has moved from its tiny Auckland studio (often referred to as a “shed” by trolls and former contestants) to filming in Portugal. “I look forward to seeing what the next thing [is] that select members of the fan base have a problem with on Reddit.” Nicholson doesn’t say it directly, but this season (airing domestically on Stan – owned by Nine, the publisher of this masthead – and internationally on co-producer World of Wonder’s own streaming platform) is Down Under’s all-in attempt not just to see its queens v the world, but to win it over too. “It’s the most Down Under experience possible: begging to be liked … but there’s no shame in asking or wanting to be seen.” Lazy Susan, judge of Drag Race Down Under vs the World The season’s cast includes season one finalist Art Simone, fellow Sydney queens Vybe, Coco Jumbo and Nikita Iman, and New Zealand’s Flor, alongside British finalist Michael Marouli, Philippines powerhouse M1ss Jade So, Spain’s Estrella Xtravaganza and American queens LaLa Ri, Nicole Paige Brooks and Raven. (I’ll come back to that last addition.) Lazy Susan, who won Down Under’s fourth season, has also joined the judging panel alongside Nicholson and host Michelle Visage. “I’ve been judging people my entire life and, finally, I’m getting paid for it,” says Lazy, speaking out of drag over Zoom, a stack of wigs behind her. “What a dream! I hope every homosexual one day experiences the monetisation of their discerning and judgmental eyes.”



Lazy Susan, Michelle Visage, Rhys Nicholson and guest judge Beks on the first episode of Drag Race Down Under vs the World. “There is some of the most immaculate drag being presented on the runway this season,” Lazy says. “I hope the camera is even able to capture the sheer level of detail and glamazonia that appears … We’ve [also] got a lot of funny girls, and that’s the lifeblood of a good Drag Race season: not just having pure glamour, but girls that can take the piss out of themselves.” Nicholson says the differences between local and US contestants are also a real highlight: “It’s a little bit messier here. Something I didn’t expect and really enjoyed this season was seeing the interactions between international and our queens, particularly Americans, because I think they’re a little more focused on imagined rules around drag. “Australian and New Zealand drag, generally speaking, is less focused on female impersonation,” Nicholson says. “It’s about this fully formed persona – meeting queens on- and off-stage or in and out of drag, they’re different people. That’s what’s fascinating to me.” It’s a US queen who has everyone talking, though. Down Under has pulled out the big guns – or big gun – with the surprise headline-generating addition of Drag Race royalty Raven to the cast. A runner-up (twice) on early US seasons who has been RuPaul’s personal make-up artist for a decade and won an Emmy Award for it, Raven’s casting would be monumental on any season. Raven is a shock inclusion in Drag Race Down Under vs the World. For the uninitiated, this is akin to Matt Corby singing covers on a rebooted Australian Idol – or maybe, to use a real-world example, chart-topping star Jessie J winning a Chinese singing competition in 2018. There’s no real logic to it, beyond the love of the game.



Naturally, speculation among the Drag Race fanbase has run wild, with theories that it’s a fake-out (something the show already did with Raven on All Stars 7) to generate viewers, even after The Hollywood Reporter confirmed she was competing. The premiere last Friday showed Raven competing like any other queen, but fans online are still suspicious. While laughing it off, Nicholson gets the disbelief. When they arrived on set, they didn’t think it was real either. Editor's pick Streaming ‘There’s been dumb luck’: Patrick Brammall on Colin, Hollywood haters and what’s next “I looked at one of the producers and was like, ‘Are you serious?’” Nicholson says. “I got them to take me behind the [Werk Room] screen when they had started filming, and was like, ‘Right, I have to go work a little harder on my make-up.’ “Seeing Raven standing on the stage was kind of panic-inducing. I’ve got to critique you, and I can see you’re clocking my face right now. You will have thoughts about my contour and how, yes, it has had to get darker since season one. My head is changing shape.” Lazy felt the same way. “Realising you’re going to be judging one of the iconic mugs of drag history is not really correct,” she says, laughing. “But you do as best you can to hold your nerve and look into the sun for as long as possible. It was crazy, but all of these divas are people that I respect so much.” Vybe, an Australian queen on Drag Race Down Under vs the World.



Expect new and familiar faces on Drag Race Down Under vs the World. Stan For all that’s changed with Down Under, it’s a case of the more things stay the same. The theories about Raven recall similar rumours about RuPaul in season one. Lighting back then was so questionable that viewers speculated the famous host wasn’t on set in Auckland but instead edited into Werk Room conversations in post-production. “It’s always something!” Nicholson says. “My thing with that was that you can’t complain about the lighting and also think we meticulously green-screened in the host of the show. They can’t happen at the same time!” Conspiracies aside, Lazy has concocted her own scheme for viewers: a continuation of her season four social media campaign to get US winner and Drag Race recapper Bob the Drag Queen to watch Down Under. While it didn’t work in 2024, she’s been messaging him on X again and might meet up soon in Los Angeles, though she admits she’s been left on read. View post on X “It’s the most Down Under experience possible,” Lazy says, laughing. “Begging to be liked. But drag inoculates you to shame. There’s no shame in asking or wanting to be seen. I didn’t put glitter on my human eyes just so you would ignore me. There’s no shame in being seen wanting things.” Drag Race Down Under vs The World streams weekly on Stan.

World.title: Check your offset account: Are the banks returning to bastardry?
World.content:
July 29, 2026 — 2:56pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It was eight years ago, during a bruising royal commission, that Australia’s banking industry sustained injury to its image so damaging that it lost the community’s trust. Now, after several years of rehabilitation efforts by the banks, behavioural creep is emerging again. The latest example is the shortchanging of hundreds of thousands of customers with mortgage offset accounts. The systemic nature of this issue was uncovered by the Australian Securities and Investments Commission. “One of the things about these … offset account failures is it’s very difficult for a customer to work out for themselves,” says ASIC chair Sarah Court. AAP The backlash from the royal commission’s revelations of banks’ bad behaviour wiped out a legion of the industry’s board directors and executives on the back of a community shaming exercise. Fast-forward to this week, and ASIC has identified that banks have recently needed to compensate borrowers to the tune of $55 million for interest they are owed.



That figure will undoubtedly rise as customers attempt to navigate the complexities of working out whether their offset savings are being accurately assessed by their bank. “One of the things about these … offset account failures is it’s very difficult for a customer to work out for themselves,” said ASIC chair Sarah Court, admitting that the amount of the potential losses to customers at this stage is completely unknown. She wouldn’t rule out that a level of complacency around behaviour may have crept back into the sector. While branding the offset problems as “structural”, it doesn’t look like the regulator is raising the issue to the level of a head-rolling offence. The banks’ defence to the shortchanging will inevitably default to these mistakes being innocent and due to deficiencies in systems and processes. In other works, they happened by accident rather than design.



Related Article Home loans Home owners warned to check offset accounts after $55 million interest issue (It’s a fair bet that if these deficient processes and systems were costing the banks money, they would have received attention, resources and rectification.) This echoes the banks’ explanations for many of the problems uncovered during the royal commission in 2018, such as the charging of fees for no service or the breaching of responsible lending obligations. Some of the more egregious behavioural issues uncovered by the royal commission were also not particularly widespread. In the banks’ latest misstep, while mortgage offset miscalculations happened to only a fraction of customers, many will be affected – there are more than 3.3 million Australians with a mortgage, after all, holding a combined $350 billion in offset accounts. The Australian Banking Industry reckons 99 per cent of those with offset accounts are paying the correct interest. But given the sheer number of accounts, 99 per cent simply isn’t good enough.



ASIC cited one case, in which a customer paid more than $3500 in extra interest in just over one month when their offset account was incorrectly delinked by their bank. In another example, two customers paid more than $17,000 in additional interest after the bank failed to inform their broker that the offset account needed to be re-linked following refinancing. One telling point about this issue needs airing: ASIC maintains that in the process of its deep dive into the eight banks surveyed, it saw no examples of customers being accidentally overcompensated. The regulator has decided against naming and shaming financial institutions caught in the offset issue. Its review didn’t cover all the banks, but covered a sample of the big four, some medium-sized lenders and smaller lenders. Some of them have been a bit tardy with redress action, others have more willingly come to the party.



So customers won’t know whom to trust. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.

World.title: ‘At least I have brand recognition’: Malcolm Roberts hits back at criticism
World.content:
PoliticsFederalPolitical leadership ‘At least I have brand recognition’: Malcolm Roberts hits back at criticism Rob Harris July 29, 2026 — 2:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Malcolm Roberts has accused the media of running a co-ordinated “hit job” against him after a series of reports highlighted the One Nation senator’s past comments praising Russian President Vladimir Putin and conspiracy theorist Alex Jones, as speculation grows over his political future. The Queensland senator used a lengthy opinion piece in The Spectator Australia to reject suggestions that he subscribes to conspiracy theories, while accusing journalists of deliberately misrepresenting his views as One Nation’s strong polling places the party under increasing scrutiny. Malcolm Roberts, pictured with One Nation colleagues Pauline Hanson, Barnaby Joyce and David Farley, praised far-right conspiracy theorist Alex Jones. Alex Ellinghausen The broadside comes after this masthead reported that Roberts said Putin had “earned his respect” by invading Ukraine, describing the war as a fight against “globalists” during a podcast appearance last year. Several reports from this masthead, The Guardian and The Australian have also revealed that Roberts stated his belief in chemtrails, posted a picture of a well-known antisemitic mural, lauded Jones as a “beacon of hope around the world” and brought up the possibility that Australia was a US corporate entity.



In his response, Roberts dismissed the reporting as politically motivated and argued that journalists had ignored his parliamentary work for years. “After a week of targeted headlines, erroneous and malicious they may be, at least I have brand recognition,” he wrote. Roberts said the articles relied on publicly available podcast interviews rather than uncovering new material, and accused media organisations of stitching together “false and misleading statements” about his beliefs. The reports have intensified attention on Roberts, one of Pauline Hanson’s closest political allies, amid growing speculation from within One Nation over whether the 71-year-old will be encouraged to step aside before the next federal election. Party figures have privately pointed to concerns about his declining health, fuelling suggestions that he could be replaced before the next poll.



He rejected claims that he endorsed chemtrail conspiracies, September 11 conspiracy theories or suggestions that the December 2025 Bondi massacre was a “false flag”. “Do I subscribe to the chemtrail conspiracy? No. That claim is false,” he wrote. “Do I subscribe to 9-11 conspiracy theories and school shootings? Of course not.” Loading Roberts also defended his repeated use of the term “globalism”, rejecting suggestions that it carried antisemitic connotations. “Since when is ‘globalism’ considered a Jewish banker conspiracy theory?” he wrote.



Jewish groups had criticised his use of the term “globalist parasites” and “globalists”, a term commonly used as a pejorative in far-right politics and in various conspiracy theories, often with antisemitic tropes. He also made no mention of his support for Putin. One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce repeatedly distanced himself from Roberts’ comments, saying they were not the views of the party, but called him a “decent man”. Related Article Political leadership Pauline Hanson has momentum. Her biggest challenge is the company she keeps While distancing himself from some of the allegations, Roberts doubled down on several controversial positions that have become central to One Nation’s platform. He declared that there were “definitely” concerns about COVID-19 vaccine safety, described net zero emissions policies as “a scam”, and said the origins of COVID-19 had been covered up. He also argued that One Nation’s growing electoral support had triggered increased attacks from political opponents and sections of the media.



“Is One Nation a threat to Labor? You bet,” he wrote. Roberts claimed that his work opposing climate policies had placed him in the sights of critics, accusing the Albanese government of wasting taxpayer money on preparations for the COP31 climate conference and calling for the abolition of the Department of Climate Change. Apart from Hanson, Roberts is one of the party’s longest-serving parliamentarians since returning to the Senate after successfully overcoming the dual citizenship crisis that briefly forced him from parliament in 2017. After securing 6.4 per cent of the primary vote at the last federal election, One Nation has enjoyed a sustained rise in support over the past six months, peaking at 29 per cent in Resolve, this masthead’s monthly polling, in June that put it ahead of both Labor and the Coalition. World.title: Gateway fires up second rig at Yandal gold find
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Gateway fires up second rig at Yandal gold find Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward July 29, 2026 — 2:41pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Gateway Mining has put its foot on the accelerator at its Yandal Gold project in Western Australia, commissioning a second reverse circulation (RC) drill rig to get to grips with its burgeoning Cowza gold discovery. The move marks a significant step-up in exploration for the company, which has in recent weeks confirmed a continuous, high-grade gold corridor at Cowza stretching over an impressive 3.5 kilometres of strike. Reverse circulation drill rig in action at Gateway Mining’s Yandal gold project 85 kilometres northeast of Wiluna in WA. The confirmation came from wide-spaced air-core drilling that demonstrated strong continuity of gold mineralisation along every drill traverse completed to date. Standout intercepts from the shallow drilling include 4 metres grading an eye-catching 11.1 grams per tonne (g/t) gold from 72m, 8m at 3.1g/t gold from 76m and 4m at 3.3g/t gold from 80m. Gateway has clearly pushed its foot on the accelerator in developing the recent discovery. Barely a week after tripling the strike length to 2.5 kilometres, the company has extended Cowza a further kilometre with the discovery’s strike expanding almost as quickly as the company can drill it.



‘The second rig enables us to test multiple areas simultaneously and rapidly assess the potential scale of the discovery.’ Gateway Mining chief executive officer Richard Pugh The mineralisation at Cowza remains open in multiple directions, with the addition of a second rig allowing the company to simultaneously test multiple areas and rapidly assess the potential scale of the discovery. The RC program has been designed to systematically drill beneath a swathe of extensive air-core gold hits to probe the system’s potential in fresh rock. The company’s flagship Yandal project, 85km north-east of Wiluna, already hosts a JORC resource of 8.17 million tonnes grading 1.52g/t gold for a solid 400,400 ounces, centred on its Horse Well gold camp and Dusk ’til Dawn deposit. Notably, that project sits in the heart of one of WA’s most revered gold provinces, the Yandal greenstone belt, just 30km south of Northern Star Resources’ long-running Jundee gold operation. The region is also home to a conga line of other world-class deposits including the Darlot-Centenary mine and Bellevue Gold’s namesake high-grade project places Gateway’s ground in the middle of one of the most sought-after exploration addresses in WA. The Cowza discovery is the latest addition to a rapidly expanding pipeline of discoveries across Gateway’s 100 kilometres of prospective gold trends. Other prospects, including Haflinger, Hummer, Mustang, Rubicon and Celia South, are creating what appears to be one of the more compelling exploration stories in the Yandal belt.



Several of these discoveries are advancing towards fresh-rock RC drilling, reflecting Gateway’s shift from making new discoveries to defining their scale and potential. Adding to the intrigue, the company says it still has a backlog of aircore assay results pending from one kilometre of drilling north of the currently defined footprint at Cowza, pointing to a steady stream of news flow in the coming weeks. Additionally, a key advantage for the company is its robust financial position. At the end of the March quarter, Gateway held a healthy $15.7 million in cash in addition to $5.6 million in liquid ASX securities, giving it a war chest of over $21 million to fund its ambitious exploration plans. Gateway Mining chief executive officer Richard Pugh said:“The commencement of a second RC rig marks an important milestone as Gateway moves into a new phase of exploration. Over the past several weeks we have demonstrated remarkable strike continuity at Cowza, with gold mineralisation now defined over approximately 3.5 kilometres and remaining open in all directions.” The company is employing a two-pronged exploration attack, bring in shallower aircore drilling to map out the mineralised footprint across its prospects before bringing in the heavier RC rigs to test for depth extensions designed to develop a better understanding of the system in the fresh unweathered rock. With an existing 400,000-ounce resource in the bag, a pipeline of new discoveries, a 3.5km long gold corridor at Cowza that is still growing, and a bank balance that would make many junior explorers blush, Gateway looks perfectly positioned to exploit any future exploration success.



Now, with the rods spinning on two rigs, it is seeking exactly that and punters will be watching closely to see how big this Yandal gold system could be. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? Contact: mattbirney@bullsnbears.com.au

World.title: Grenades, military-grade weapons seized from alleged Sydney safehouse
World.content:
NationalNSWCrime Grenades, military-grade weapons seized from alleged Sydney safehouse Daniel Lo Surdo Updated July 29, 2026 — 2:39pm ,first published July 29, 2026 — 7:24am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Grenades, military-grade weapons, more than 1000 rounds of ammunition and $3 million worth of drugs were uncovered in an alleged Sydney safehouse when the state’s anti-gang detectives raided the suburban property on Tuesday, raising renewed concerns about the spread of firearms in the city months after gun reforms passed the parliament. Taskforce Falcon detectives raided the Glenfield property on Tuesday morning, where they discovered six grenades, three semi-automatic weapons, four shotguns and a pistol. Six kilograms of cocaine, 15 kilograms of cannabis, 1.1 kilograms of heroin, 107 grams of MDMA, a kilogram of ketamine and $9000 in cash were also seized. Loading A 26-year-old man, dressed in black track pants and T-shirt, was led from the property in handcuffs, clutching a gold vape in his hand, before being taken to Campbelltown Police Station in a police truck. He was charged with a range of offences, including possessing a dangerous weapon with intent to injure, possessing more than three unregistered firearms without a licence, three counts of supplying a drug greater than a commercial quantity, and knowingly dealing with the proceeds of crime. The man was refused bail to appear at Campbelltown Local Court on Wednesday.



A 26-year-old woman, led from the alleged safehouse by a plain-clothed police officer, was charged with organising, conducting and assisting at a drug premises, and was bailed ahead of a court appearance in Campbelltown next month. Several firearms and gun parts were discovered in a black duffle bag hidden in the alleged safehouse. NSW Police Police will allege the pair are contract criminals who have provided services, including the use of their property to stow weapons and drugs, for a range of underworld groups. Assistant Commissioner Scott Cook said the discovery of grenades and military-grade weapons was of particular concern. He suggested that Tuesday’s seizure was an example of “proactive [police] work” preventing a violent crime. NSW Police Minister Yasmin Catley said it was “awful to think what could have happened” if detectives failed to seize the weapons from the alleged safehouse.



Three grenades were found at the property. NSW Police “We do not want to see these weapons in our communities, and thanks to the hard work of police, they are now out of the hands of criminals,” Catley said. Police were continuing to investigate the source of the weapons on Wednesday. Cook said the grenades seized are the same class as those used in the Australian and US armies, and would’ve “almost demolished” the suburban home if detonated. The state government rushed through gun reforms on Christmas Eve last year, less than two weeks after gunmen shot dead 15 people celebrating Hanukkah at Bondi Beach. The new laws implemented new limits on the number of firearms an individual can own – four, or 10 for farmers and sporting shooters – and also sought to strengthen firearms licence checks and oversight mechanisms.



Taskforce Falcon was launched by NSW Police in May last year to crush simmering gangland conflicts across the city’s streets. It has been responsible for 683 arrests, leading to more than 1700 charges. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘Very large distaste’: ICAC told of efforts to damage MP, building commissioner
World.content:
NSW Liberal operatives prepared a “shit sheet” about former police minister David Elliott while a senior ministerial staffer circulated an allegedly damaging video about then-building commissioner David Chandler as part of a concerted campaign to end their careers. The Independent Commission Against Corruption on Wednesday continued hearing evidence from one-time Catholic Schools NSW employee Dylan Whitelaw, where he detailed how the right-wing of the Liberals had a “very large distaste” for Elliott, a factional enemy who belongs to the party’s centre-right. Dylan Whitelaw arrives at the NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) on Wednesday morning. Kate Geraghty Whitelaw, who was a member of the religious conservative group the NSW Reformers, said the right’s objection to Elliott was behind its motivation in preparing a dirt sheet, which included claims of an extramarital affair, about the former Baulkham Hills MP. He later conceded that the dirt sheet was likely prepared to “further certain interests” of fugitive Sydney developer Jean Nassif, who is at the centre of the ICAC’s inquiry.



“At the time, it would appear to me as just standard factional warfare. On reflection, absolutely, that’s what it appears to be,” Whitelaw said. The 25-year-old, who worked in the office of then-planning minister Anthony Roberts after leaving Catholic Schools NSW, also revealed the efforts made to have Chandler sacked as building commissioner. Former minister David Elliott was a target of the Reformers faction, the ICAC has heard. Jessica Hromas Roberts’ former chief of staff Chris Spence wanted then-fair trading minister Eleni Petinos to raise a video in an upcoming budget estimates hearing, with the ultimate goal of damaging Chandler’s career, Whitelaw said. The video, Whitelaw said, allegedly included the imputation Chandler was “racist” and included a reference to a list of building certifiers and developers he had given to banks.



“I believe his [Spence’s] words were something to the effect of, ‘We’ve just got to get rid of this guy’,” Whitelaw said. Whitelaw told the commission that Spence and Petinos were “close”, but did not know why she would want to have Chandler dismissed. Whitelaw said Spence later complained that Petinos had “f---ed it up” by not raising the video in her budget estimates appearance. Petinos, who is a frontbencher in Liberal Leader Kellie Sloane’s shadow cabinet, is on maternity leave, and Sloane has said she would not be commenting on Petinos’ potential involvement in the ICAC inquiry. As part of its wide-ranging investigation, the ICAC is probing whether political donations were made by Nassif, who has fled to Lebanon, to Liberal Party operatives Christian Ellis and Jeremy Greenwood to, among other things, damage Elliott’s political career.





He later acknowledged that claims of Elliott’s affair were likely to be false. The commission heard on Tuesday claims that Federal Liberal Leader Angus Taylor had pledged a $15,000 donation, and regular $3000 payments, to support the NSW Reformers. Whitelaw said he had been told about this promise by McInerney, who also chaired the right-wing faction at the time. Related Investigation

Investigation Inside Operation Rosny Taylor, who said he was not involved in the inquiry, initially told the media donations were an issue for the NSW Liberals head office, but on Wednesday he denied making a contribution to the NSW Reformers, stressing that “no payment was made”. Whitelaw told the commission there was a contract between Catholic Schools NSW and Beckington, however he said it was more accurately “an arrangement” with the understanding minimal consulting work would be done for the education body, and instead, activities would be undertaken to further the interests of the Reformers.



Curtin asked Whitelaw on Wednesday: “Are you able to say whether there’s a connection between the monthly amount that Angus Taylor had indicated to Mr McInerney that he’s prepared to make, and the corresponding increase, or [what] appears to be an increase, that happened at the same time in the amount that Catholic Schools NSW was paying to Beckington?” Whitelaw: “No, I wouldn’t be able to talk to that”. The inquiry continues on Thursday. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Oil and gas giant becomes one of Australia’s biggest winners from Iran war
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesEnergy Oil and gas giant becomes one of Australia’s biggest winners from Iran war Nick Toscano Updated July 29, 2026 — 1:53pm ,first published 1:51pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australia’s largest oil and gas producer, Woodside Energy, has emerged as one of the nation’s biggest corporate beneficiaries of the Iran war, reporting nearly a 30 per cent revenue jump to $6 billion over the past three months. As the conflict in the Middle East pushes the world deeper into an energy crisis, Woodside’s quarterly sales update on Wednesday offers one of the clearest signs yet that surging fossil fuel prices are delivering major earnings boosts to exporters that operate outside the Persian Gulf, whose cargoes have become increasingly valuable as buyers seek reliable alternative supplies. Woodside’s Pluto gas plant, near Karratha. Woodside Demand and prices for shipments of super-chilled liquefied natural gas (LNG) – one of Australia’s most lucrative exports – have surged since Iran launched missile strikes on a key Qatari LNG hub and disrupted tanker movements through the Strait of Hormuz, the vital trade corridor that normally carries about a fifth of global LNG supplies. Countries across Asia that usually rely on Qatari LNG to power their homes, factories and electric grids are desperate to find replacement cargoes to head off shortfalls. Customers have been increasingly turning to Australia – the world’s third-largest supplier of LNG, behind Qatar – to make up for the drop-off.



Woodside chief executive Liz Westcott said the LNG crunch had driven up prices and lifted the company’s sales revenue despite modestly lower production volumes across the quarter. “Revenue is up, prices are up,” she said. “The LNG market very much relies on the Middle East – Qatari volumes are 20 per cent of the global supply, and that’s been constrained completely.” However, higher prices have also begun to erode demand. Some price-sensitive buyers in Asia had sought to shield themselves from soaring energy costs and had moved to lower their LNG consumption this year, including by switching back to dirtier sources of energy, such as coal-fired power stations, Westcott said. “You’ve seen fuel-switching in Asia to reduce demand as prices increase,” she said.



Some analysts have warned that this year’s upheaval in the LNG market may have lasting consequences for demand for the fuel. For the second time in four years, Asian nations have been reminded of the risks of their heavy exposure to LNG, including price shocks and shortages amid geopolitical turmoil. In 2022, LNG prices hit unprecedented highs following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Related Article Energy Gas giants to reap $18 billion war windfall, reviving export tax calls However, Woodside did not expect a long-term LNG demand reduction, Westcott said. Instead, Australian LNG suppliers could stand to benefit further in future if Asian LNG buyers reconsidered their heavy reliance on Middle Eastern suppliers and pivoted towards trade partners perceived as more geopolitically stable, she said. “We are seeing customers are recognising the benefits of diversification of supply,” Westcott said. “Our proximity to Asia puts us in a really good place.” This year’s LNG prices and sales revenue could also strengthen Australia’s budget outlook. Before the outbreak of the war on February 28, the federal government had anticipated a sharp decline in LNG export income from producers in Queensland, Western Australia and the Northern Territory. Official forecasters had projected revenue to slip from more than $50 billion to $47 billion in the 2027 financial year, dragged down by an impending wave of new LNG projects in the United States and Qatar that had threatened to drive the market into oversupply.



Instead, the latest government projections, released earlier this month, reveal that LNG revenue is now expected to climb from $59 billion in the 2026 financial year to $65 billion in 2027 – an increase of $18 billion compared with previous forecasts. “A cessation of LNG output from Qatar due to military conflict has pushed LNG prices up sharply and raised price forecasts,” the report from the federal Industry Department said. The revised forecast lands as the prospect of mega-profits in the gas industry fuels a political debate in Canberra. Climate groups, crossbench MPs and unions are pushing for higher taxes on multinational energy giants, arguing that the current federal offshore oil and gas tax – the Petroleum Resource Rent Tax (PRRT) – fails to deliver a fair public return. The Albanese government has previously rejected independent senator David Pocock’s popular campaign to impose a 25 per cent tax on gas export revenue.
